The development of advanced isochronous mass spectrometry techniques relies on precise determination of the $A$-dependent correction factor for the magnetic rigidity of cyclotron masses, accomplished through the combination of individual and collective deceleration methods.  This research introduces an innovative approach to mass measurement that utilizes the relativistic energy and momentum of highly ionized nuclei to accurately determine the $B\rho$-mass relation.  By doing so, it obviates the need for the $A$-dependent correction factor, which can be complicated and uncertain.  Instead, it necessitates a more straightforward correction factor that relates electric rigidity to magnetic rigidity, largely free from uncertainty.  Furthermore, it enables the precise application of time-of-flight corrections, which accounts for the slight variations in revolution frequencies based on the specific characteristics of each nucleus.  Consequently, it allows for more accurate mass measurements, particularly for heavier and less ionized nuclei, and may expand the capabilities of this technique to include radioactive nuclei with as few as 10 electrons.
This note serves as a concise introduction to standardizing flows in lattice field theories.

The primary objective of Structured Text Recognition (STR) is to identify text that adheres to predefined patterns, such as phone numbers and dates, within a broader context. While recent breakthroughs in Standard Text Recognition (STR) have leveraged Improved Transformer (Transformer) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), the specific requirements of STR tasks pose significant challenges for these approaches, such as character class ambiguity and variant recognition rules. To tackle these obstacles, researchers aim to incorporate structural constraints into Standard Text recognition models to refine predictions and enhance accuracy. In an effort to explore this possibility, the current study investigates influencing reader networks with the patterns specified through regular expressions, with the goal of improving STR performance on publicly available datasets: ICDAR2013MD fields and ICDAR2017PCP.

A novel strategy for producing top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions is proposed, 
leveraging the distinct characteristics of gluon saturation.  Initial top quark 
production occurs at a high rapidity, with the process dominated by the 
interaction between the proton and the nucleus.  The nucleus emits a virtual 
quark-antiquark pair, with the quark undergoing a rapid fragmentation into a 
top quark, while the antiquark is absorbed by the proton.  The proposed detection 
method involves measuring the nuclear and lepton-like forward particles and 
identifying the mutual back-to-back angular distribution, which provides a 
potential top quark production signature.

In cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks, the complex interpretation process of converting user queries into SQL statements can be bypassed by training a single deep learning model to directly map from the user queries to the SQL statements, thereby eliminating the need for a two-step process. Although this approach has demonstrated strong results, it often fails to generalize well when the training and testing datasets have different domains, a critical limitation.

To address this challenge, existing solutions incorporate two additional constraints into the model to mitigate the domain shift effect and enhance generalization performance. However, these constraints have been designed based on domain experts' knowledge, thereby limiting their potential.

This study explores the use of auxiliary tasks as an effective means of enhancing cross-domain text-to-SQL model performance.

Specifically, a comprehensive evaluation of various auxiliary tasks is conducted, a new meta-task auxiliary task is introduced, and two domain-adversarial training objectives are developed for the auxiliary tasks, thereby facilitating the cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic interpretation process. Experimental findings demonstrate that auxilary tasks can significantly improve cross-domain SQL semantic interpretation performance and that our multi-class auxiliary task-based approach yields superior results in comparison to existing methods.

The frequency range of the Low Frequency Archive is distinct from other large-scale structure surveys, allowing us to probe a less explored part of the baryonic matter distribution function. We present our findings of the galaxy power spectrum and bias in the context of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey's first data release. We covered approximately 300 million galaxies with redshifts exceeding 0.2, spanning the North Galactic Cap to the North Pole. Our survey's limitations are primarily due to survey boundaries and signal fluctuations due to galaxy positioning relative to the galaxy's bright centre. We leverage an extensive set of cross-matched galaxy samples against the UKIDSS Ultra Deep Survey to create comprehensive redshift and mass profiles, including 104 quasar samples of various magnitudes. We discuss how our quasas exhibit a consistent evolutionary pattern, which differs when compared using projected density or redshift-space distortion-adjusted clustering measures. Our findings also reveal that passive galaxy models are insufficient to fully account for galaxy distribution. We provide galaxy samples that match the USDS' infrared luminosity, demonstrating a pattern of stronger large-scale structure influence compared to an SDSS sample. Our results also indicate a possible change in the effect of large-scale structure on galaxy distribution when considering luminosity. Our analysis also includes a possible connection between galaxy colours and their influence from large-scale structure, as well as a preliminary examination of galaxy–inferred dark matter halos' halo mass-dependent bias.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model serves as a robust alternative to the traditional Lasso in scenarios involving outliers or noisy data. Unlike the absolute loss commonly used with Lasso, the HDR Lasso employs the rank loss function, making it suitable for handling data integrity issues. The convergence properties of the HDR Lasso are proven, and to efficiently solve this non-smooth and non-linear optimization problem, a hybrid adaptive-sieving algorithm is developed, combining the adaptive-thresholding and the l1-norm analysis. Numerical experiments in simulations and real-world data analysis demonstrate that the algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed and accuracy of variable selection.

In response to growing interest for understanding the concept of entropy generation among physicists, we provide an extensive review focused on equilibrium and non-equilibrium states of quantum systems. By utilizing the framework developed by Salsburg specifically for quantum mechanics, where entropy generation remains finite even in tightly bound systems, we explore various scenarios and discuss the implications of multiple选择的 definition of entropy. Furthermore, these definitions are applied to both finite and infinite systems and we explore the region of temporal equilibrium and the implications of weak driving on entropy generation, revealing the region of negative entropy generation under certain circumstances. Our analysis reveals that for the study of entropy generation in the non-equilibrium regime, where the system's Hamiltonian is time-dependent, new methods and techniques are required.

Over the past decade, Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies such as automation and deep learning have experienced significant growth, largely due to their capacity to minimize human labor required for complex tasks, including their use in visual analysis. Although this has provided organizations with the ability to leverage the capacity-enhancing properties of AI, very few studies have investigated the environmental consequences associated with this technology, specifically its ability to replace human labor. We examined the environmental effects of AI in three categories: (1) the environmental cost of AI itself, (2) the environmental benefits provided by AI, and ( (3) the environmental savings resulting from AI replacing human work. Our analysis revealed that AI's environmental cost far outweighs its benefits, largely due to the high energy consumption required for AI software development and the electronic equipment it necessitates. In contrast, the environmental savings resulting from AI replacing human work far exceed its benefits, specifically in scenarios involving labor-intensive electronic device assembly.

Research into prescriptive procedure monitoring has been conducted for quite some time, yet the field's current state is not clear. We aim to resolve this ambiguity by creating a classification system that categorizes prescriptive procedure monitoring research based on their key characteristics. The framework, which considers the underlying research question, real-world setting, process being monitored, analysis techniques, and metrics used, allows for structured comparisons across studies. Upon reviewing 39 relevant papers from the last three decades, we found that existing monitoring research often struggles to accurately predict actual performance due to limited real-world testing and a lack of comprehensive results. Furthermore, there appears to be little progression in terms of methods used, potentially hindering a clear understanding of prescriptive procedure monitoring's capabilities. The proposed framework can help guide future research and highlight key areas for improvement.

A generalized Boussinesq model governing heated material flow with a fixed pressure field is utilized in this research. The model is validated through comparison of its predictions with real-world molten sand data, and the results demonstrate its capability to accurately predict complex flow patterns. The study employs an adaptive, back-looking error estimation approach to compute the temperature and velocity fields, and accurately control the error during control volume calculations. This approach is demonstrated by simulating an adaptive flow analysis in an experimental molten sand oven. The analysis shows that the proposed method is effective in managing errors and is suitable for applications requiring high-prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the study reveals that the convective and diffusive contributions significantly influence the control volume calculations, and their relative importance varies depending on the flow conditions.

Machine learning's stacking ensemble method boasts strong predictive capabilities.
The idea is to combine diverse models in two steps. First, a first set of models,
called level 1 models, predict outcomes for given data points. Then, a second set, level 2, uses these predictions as their input and tries to predict outcomes,
taking the level 1 models' predictions into account. We've developed a mathematical framework, a stacking formulation, to study the relationships between the models and data.
Our analysis shows that this stacking formulation can be derived from well-known results in linear algebra.
Based on this formulation, we've defined nuclear stacking, a new category of stacking problems.
Level 1 models are viewed as vectors in a nuclear space, with their coordinates representing their features.
We've studied how many of these coordinates level 1 models need.
Our findings show that, on average, there are O(n^1.5) coordinates, with some problems possibly having as many as O(n^2).
This leads to the conclusion that neural networks are not suitable for stacking formulation due to the number of coordinates they present.
We've also developed an algorithm for solving nuclear stacking formulation, with its runtime depending on the number of coordinates, as well as on other parameters. Our analysis shows this runtime to be optimal.

Societal views can be modeled through the lens of structural balance within social networks, where opinions and relationships are considered favorable or unfavorable from an individual's perspective. This study addresses the balance of preferences among a group of individuals, examining how the balance of limits exists within a dynamic social framework where a single person's opinions and preferences change simultaneously. Through a detailed analysis of possible configurations of opinions and preferences, this study shows that as the range of possible structures of feelings expands, so does the possible range of balances of limits of opinions and preferences, suggesting a possible connection between the balance of limits and a parameter representing the proportion of positive relationships within a group, known as the bias. Furthermore, this study explores how the balance of limits shifts when a group of individuals expresses stronger positive or negative views. We demonstrate that as the strength of negative views increases, the number of possible structures of feelings increases significantly, while the number of possible structures of feelings decreases significantly as the strength of positive views increases. Additionally, this study explores how the balance of limits changes when individuals' views are flipped, noting that a flip can expand or reduce the range of possible structures of feelings, depending on its nature.

We investigate a type of matter described by the state equation $p=c_s^2\rho$, which models the internal dynamics of asymptotically flat, static systems in four-dimensional Einstein's theory with matter fields that carry no electric charge. Our analysis reveals that this specific state equation and the considered field equations support unique, regular solutions representing massive objects with no horizon, featuring a scalar field with non-zero values at the center that smoothly transition to zero at infinity. Additionally, we develop a set of ODEs to study small fluctuations within this system, which we show has a corresponding infinite set of zero-frequency modes characterized by polynomials, indicating a unique relationship between the object's mass, radius, and scalar field configuration that diverges from the predictions of quantized scalar fields in quantized spacetime models.

One essential aspect of RNA production is the time delay associated with RNA polymerase activity, which is frequently overlooked in current RNA transcription models. This study develops a comprehensive framework for analyzing delay-differential equations in RNA transcription modeling. The framework enables seamless integration of precise spike functions in delay-differential equations, smooth incorporation of oscillatory functions, and the use of smoothlee delayed terms to model transcription. Furthermore, a public repository is provided for delay-differential equation models of gene expression, which complements the traditional ordinary differential equation-based genome-transcriptome models. The framework's utility is demonstrated through its application to three RNA transcription scenarios: (a) simple, passive delay in single gene transcription, (b) active transcription optimization through delayed feedback in the Arabidopsis thaliana curcurbita transcription, and (c) transcription of multiple genes co-regulated by a delayed time, which is illustrated by the STRA7 gene in the GC box. The results reveal that considering RNA production delays yields more accurate predictions of gene expression patterns, which may have significant implications for understanding genetic regulation.

Recent studies of the electric transition probabilities between low-spin, shape-coexisting states in 64Ni have led to a crucial finding - a zero-spin spin-zero state. To investigate the impact of this state on 64Ni, a modified three-body monopole force was incorporated into the nuclear Hamiltonian, in addition to conventional delocalization effects. Calculated energy levels and electromagnetic transitions using the modified force showed satisfactory agreement with experimental data, in contrast to previous models which failed to match the data. Notably, including the modified three-body monopole force made the previously calculated triaxial state's angular momentum state inconsistent with experimental observations.

Chiral SU(Nc) SQCD with Nf (where Nf is greater than or equal to 2) flavors exhibits a variety of dualities that are challenging to verify through direct comparison of the theories' infrared properties. To address this, we explore the dangling bag, a model proposed to describe the low-energy behavior of chiral SU(Nc) SQCD with Nf flavors. By analyzing the F-terms of a set of Nf monopole superfields, we derive a proposed duality for chiral SU(Nc) SQCD with Nf flavors. This involves a theory with USp(2Nf - 2) gauge symmetry and Nc chiral doublet superfields. Our analysis supports the theory for the specified range of Nf, with the hope of resolving long-standing standing orders.

A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, S)$ is formed when the direct sum of codes $C$ and $S$ results in the entire free module $R^n$, specifically $C \oplus S = R^n$. Researchers have found a method to transform each element of the quotient group $G/\Phi(G)$ into a polynomial over the integer ring $\mathbb{Z}$, and subsequently developed the Davenport constant's application in determining the LPC of cyclic group codes over $\mathbb{Z}$. A similar strategy is employed for ideals of finite rank in the quotient group $G$, leading to results regarding the LPC of group codes over finite ideal rings, the ideal complement property of Davenport constant and its variation on prime cyclic group ideals, and the application of these results to the study of additive complements of $\mathbb{Z}m$-periodic sequences.

We introduce a novel function representation, tailored for probabilistic inference, that significantly accelerates complex calculations like finding the most probable explanation and solving constrained optimisation problems in graphical models. Specifically, it enables O(N) time complexity in undirected models and P(d)*N in directed models, where N is the number of variables, d is the maximum function arity, and P(d) is a function that grows with arity. Conversely, a widely used method, constraint relaxation, operates in undirected models with undetermined time complexity and a lower bound of d with arity undirected functions, in directed models.

We address the challenge of identifying large items that are partially or completely obscured within a video feed, even when they are misaligned in time and space. This task is critical for applications such as tracking the whereabouts of missing persons. Our proposed method synchronizes audio and visual data in an unsupervised manner, reducing the computational load by processing information asynchronously. This enhances the system's robustness and resilience during the tracking process. Moreover, we introduce an efficient and lightweight entropy-based approach to address the issue of drift, offering a more affordable and scalable alternative to existing methods. Our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance when tested on the Enron, Volleyball, and Cityuser datasets.

Suspension flow behavior changes dramatically and suddenly as thickness increases, but the precise factors behind its thickness and the overlap of two different thickness regimes remain unclear. To gain insight, researchers measured the overall suspension structure, from microscopic to macroscopic levels, as it went through its transition to increased thickness. They found that suspensions of massive particles, which undergo significant structural changes, display similar structure evolution regardless of variations in key parameters, leading to a new classification based on a single gauge for predicting and comparing this abrupt transition.

This research aims to address the hourly tracking of electricity consumption patterns in Pakistan in response to the natural gas disruption triggered by the construction of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. To this end, we gather and analyze data from the Pakistan Electricity Authority, focusing on the country's largest power supplier, with our dataset spanning from 2014 to 2019. By identifying key factors such as daylight hours, temperature, and the season, we build predictive models for electricity consumption within each hour of the day. The methods we employ include ordinary least squares (OLS), ridge regression, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), with our results indicating that LASSO to be the most effective approach in capturing the tracking of electricity consumption.

As Google's personalisation technology gathers more user data, its impact on search result composition has raised ethical concerns. There is a risk that the dependence on the personalised algorithm could affect the diversity of search results, catering too closely to users' existing views. This effect could lead to information cocoons, hindering individuals from discovering and processing new information, and consequently impair decision-making. This study seeks to investigate the extent to which search results are tailored based on user profiles, and the implications this may have on the amount of relevant search results missed. Empirical evidence is gathered through a series of web searches conducted using the same query by different participants with different backgrounds, and the results demonstrate that, on average, individuals miss about 10-20\% of the relevant search results due to the influence of Google's personalisation. Furthermore, the study finds that missing relevant search results tends to increase the time it takes for participants to make decisions and the level of uncertainty associated with those decisions.

Automatically creating software pipelines from graphical flow charts is a complex task, as the resulting pipelines can be thought of as graphs. Our approach, Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN), uses a deep learning method to predict the edges in the pipeline graph based on the flow chart. This is achieved by training the network to take flow chart images as input and produce corresponding graph representations, like those generated with Graphviz. However, the training data for such configurations is unlabelled, so we employed an self-supervised learning technique where nodes are randomly removed to create supertasks, allowing the network to predict the removed nodes based on the remaining graph. Our results show that the various supertasks combined provide better accuracy than using a single supertask alone.

This text explores multiple reduction techniques used in climate dynamics, continuing a follow-up to the author's 2013 Ph.D. dissertation. It summarizes and potentially revises the key points from the work presented in the document known as arXiv:1305.3813v4.

The development of radiation-hydrodynamics codes that can accurately simulate the dynamical properties of kilonova ejecta is crucial for predicting the light curves of binary neutron star mergers. To achieve this, an accurate opacities model is required, which is heavily dependent on the atomic data of the relevant elements. In this study, we are focused on the development of such a model and the accurate atomic data needed to support it. Our work involves obtaining relativistic, bound-state energies and wavefunctions for the Os isoelectronic sequence, spanning from Au IV to Os VIII. Using these wavefunctions, we calculate both two-electron and three-electron bound-continuum cross sections, allowing us to assemble complete atomic models. These models take into consideration the rich fine and hyperfine structure and the isomer structure present in the Os isoelectronic sequence. The accuracy of our calculations is validated by comparing the obtained atomic data with the results from the NIST atomic spectra database. The outcomes of this study will contribute significantly in several areas, such as the simulation of ejecta properties in neutron star mergers, improving the accuracy of solar abundance estimates, and enhancing the understanding of the complex atomic structure in keV plasma environments.

This study explores the efficiency of using automated deep learning techniques for segmenting the stomach, intestines, and liver on CT scans. Our findings indicate that a trained U-Net model, with pre-optimized parameters, can be deployed on edge computing devices like the Jetson Nano for real-time application. However, to prevent over-training and improve generalization, a few key adjustments were made. K-fold cross-validation was utilized to validate the model, with stomach and intestine images split into training and testing sets. For the liver, full cross-validation was performed, involving training and testing on different datasets. Our results show that for CT scan images, kernel smoothing and bias correction significantly boosted model accuracy, resulting in improved performance metrics such as an improved Dice coefficient and reduced Hausdorff distance for stomach and intestine images. Moreover, these techniques demonstrated comparable performance to control images, albeit with slightly lower Dice coefficients. Our liver analysis revealed successful model convergence and nearly identical performance metrics to control images, with a p-value > 0.05 indicating negligible differences. Our study confirms that deep learning models can be used to automatically identify and segment organs on medical imaging, with excellent efficiency and accuracy.

Compositional analysis is an advanced statistical technique used to examine and interpret the compositions of samples. Traditional linear algebra concepts are extended in the compositional framework to include the examination of sample sets. Key comparisons between traditional and compositional assessments involve mean vectors, covariance matrices, and principal component analysis. Kullback-Leibler divergences replace Euclidean distances in the compositional paradigm, and the approach is thoroughly illustrated using the analysis of compositional datasets.

We analyzed a comprehensive dataset of exoplanets discovered through radial velocity techniques, specifically those within the CORALIE/HARPS sample, in search of factors influencing detection probabilities and the aforementioned 'wasteland' region. This combination of parameters, including minimum mass, stellar mass, orbital period, and eccentricity, best fits our analysis, with detection probabilities also considering signal characteristics, as well as the eccentricity of orbits. Our findings indicate that currently discovered planets in this sample tend to fall within or beyond the 'wasteland' region, with host stars possessing masses $\lesssim 1.25\ M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Furthermore, considering potential biases, such as those related to detection probabilities and unsaturated magnetic signals, along with evolutionary hypotheses, including core-accretion models, may help to explain the apparent absence of planets in the 'wasteland' region.

Achieving reliable automated attention control in AI systems mimics human attention control mechanisms, which is essential for creating more human-like AI. Human attention control allows us to focus on relevant aspects of complex tasks and filter out unnecessary information, minimizing cognitive load. This paper proposes a new model that mimics this process, using a information-theoretic approach to balance attention between relevant and non-relevant task components. The proposed model maximizes the amount of information extracted from focused components while ensuring that no sensitive details are revealed, which can be evaluated using mutual information. Notably, this model falls within the deep learning family of efficient coding principles, which seek to minimize redundancy, and our findings support this connection in a more formal and structured way.

The first option is least preferred due to stringent constraints from experiments.
Dark matter interacting with the top quark could be directly detected by next-generation experiments.
However, neutron-related interactions were previously overlooked in theoretical studies.
This research explores compressed dark matter scenarios where dark matter particles have low mass and interact via a narrow mass range with the Higgs, top quark, or neutron.
While the ground state of dark matter particles is stable, those with slightly higher mass can decay into them through the virtual interaction of a top quark or Higgs boson.
The reverse process is also possible, where dark matter particles interact with a neutron to yield a neutron and a virtual top quark or Higgs boson.
Due to their low mass, dark matter particles can be highly abundant and form compact states.
Their interaction with nuclei can result in the emission of photons, providing a potential signal for the study of dark matter.
The research reveals that, while the top quark interaction makes a notable contribution to photon production in dark matter states, the low mass range of dark matter particles allows a significant increase of about two orders of magnitude in photon production compared to the top quark interaction alone.
This photon emission can be highly preferred in certain conditions, where it may significantly exceed that from the top quark interaction.

Recurrent neural networks, when made large enough, can match the performance of fully connected models, like multi-layer perceptrersners, in various tasks. However, the advantages of RNNs over such models, especially in the simpler case, have remained unclear. To address this question, our study focuses on solving a 1D version of the neurobiological learning problem: creating models that learn quickly. We discovered that a specific type of RNN model, the fully-connected SDRRNN, outperforms other simplified models and brings it closer to the complexity of neural networks with synapses based on local rules. The model's sparse weight matrix has a unique update mechanism that significantly reduces the complexity of its learning process. The comparison of our findings with local rule-based models like the gridworld LPNN shows a notable lag in the latter's performance.

This work delves into a particular class of nilpotent algebras and investigates their multiplications using a formal approach to explore various algebraic properties through a geometry of associators. Specifically, it represents left-nilpotent and right-nilpotent conditions using equations involving the associator, while generalizing the Gelfand-Avramov theory on the associator's zero locus. Furthermore, it extends the concepts of Gelfand-Avramov and Lebedinsky on the categorification of this geometry, proving that the general linear group acts transitively on specific varieties of nilpotent algebras of a given dimension. This demonstrates that all such algebras are isomorphic under certain conditions based on dimension. The article also explores the connection between algebraic nilpotency and associators, categorifies this connection, and examines the Fitting's lemma through the lens of the associator.

High-redshift Active Galactic Nuclei jets are studied through radio and X-ray emissions. To gain a comprehensive understanding, one must also consider thermal bremsstrahlung emissions. We conducted research on the impact of CMB radiation on these galactic nuclei by performing 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations at high resolution. It was observed that the thermal feedback from CMB increases jet collimation and power output in the form of radiation, but has a relatively minor effect on the mass flow and jet power at high redshifts due to radiation's relatively small role. Nevertheless, this effect becomes more pronounced as the redshift increases. Our results also indicate that this radiation leads to the formation of complex, bi-modal velocity and temperature patterns within jets. Furthermore, it has been found that jets are noticeably more radiative and exhibit a distinct spectral signature in the infrared and radio bands as a result of this phenomenon. Power spectral density measurements indicate a characteristic break in the radio spectrum at a specific frequency, which is determined by redshift and synchrotron radiation efficiency. This break frequency shifts to lower frequencies at higher redshifts, but it may rise again at extremely high redshifts, potentially reaching values as high as $10^{17}$ Hz, where the jets transition from nonthermal to thermal spectra, resulting in a change in the high-frequency slope of the jet spectrum from a $-6$ to a $-5$ slope. A variety of gravity models can be expressed in a single, unified framework: any such model is either cinetic or non-cinetic, depending on whether the associated function's second derivative is proportional to the first, or not. We explore a standardized lagrangian formulation for cinetic models, demonstrating its equivalence to their original forms. We also derive standardized options for specific types of graviton kinetic functions. We then turn to non-cinetic models, establishing specific requirements for consistent cosmological term formulation. We derive general methods for this requirement, with a focus on achieving this goal through both the standard and modified formulation methods. We apply these methods to specific classes of non-cinetic models, including those based on the curvature tensor, the square of the no-kinetic function, and certain other constructions.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry, making it suitable for high-precision image alignment in diverse medical subfields.  Traditional feature-based registration techniques struggle with symmetry, as evident in heart alignments.  The proposed method leverages a symmetry-invariant feature by considering the average of cardiac orientations in various directions, resulting in more robust and invariant descriptors.  The proposed descriptors are combined with 3D SIFT features to create more comprehensive and rotation-invariant descriptors.  The proposed method demonstrates superior performance on synthetic and real medical image datasets, achieving lower alignment errors compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

We analyzed the complete set of photometric observations from our study on the binary star SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which aligns with our previous findings and confirms its 40.5-minute period. This study reveals that the secondary star in the binary has a mass of approximately 0.57 times that of our sun, while the primary star's size has increased compared to our earlier study. Additionally, we found evidence suggesting the presence of a third body in the binary system. To further understand the nature of binary stars with short periods, we have placed our results in the context of the broader binary star population.

In deep neural networks, two prevalent methods for pooling features are max pooling and average pooling, though their efficacy remains undisputed despite widespread use. We investigate these pooling operations within the optimal transport framework, revealing that max pooling corresponds to the $L_1$-optimal transport, while average pooling represents the $L_1_2$-optimal transport. Both of these are distinct forms of the optimal transport with a linear cost. Our research also introduces a generalised form of the $L_p$-optimal transport with a quadratic cost function. We derive the dual problem for this new POQ, leveraging the Kantorovich duality. Our findings suggest that this new POQ can be effectively solved using existing solvers without incurring additional computational costs, offering a promising approach for overcoming obstacles in optimal transport with a large number of sources.

The application of the Optical Classification Scheme for Active Galactic Nuclei classification allows for a detailed comparison among active galaxies with different types of activity. This study employs K-band images from the SDSS database and optical spectra from the ZOO sample to analyze active galaxies. By combining the Optical Classification Scheme with the morphological classification, we are able to examine host galaxy characteristics and their properties for each activity type. Furthermore, this method enables us to investigate whether activity orientation influences host galaxy properties and their characteristics. By comparing galaxies with different activity levels, we identify that spirals are more prevalent in active galaxies than other galaxy types, although this trend diminishes among supermassive black holes exceeding 10^8 solar masses. Additionally, we observe that star-forming galaxies are more prevalent as hosts for type 1 active galaxies, while passive galaxies are more likely to host type 2 active galaxies. This study also indicates that host galaxy differences between type 1 and type 2 active galaxies are more pronounced than those between orientation classes, suggesting that host galaxy differences and active galaxy activity type differences are likely correlated.

This paper characterizes rotational surfaces in E^4 with a 1-type Gaussian map at each point. 
It's established that if a rotationally symmetric surface has a 1-type Gaussian map at each point, then it can be either a specific type of cylindrical surface, or the rotation profile curve must satisfy a specific differential equation, with two possible solutions for its rotation coordinate.

Neural networks that estimate depth unilaterally have seen significant advancements recently, leading to applications in various high-level vision tasks. This study examines the potential of using depth estimation as a novel image representation for training semantic segmentation models. We assess the effectiveness of depth estimates in capturing spatial object characteristics for segmentation, comparing the performance of a depth-based approach with traditional pre-training methods. Our results from the Cityscape dataset reveal that a model based on depth estimation surpasses a model pre-trained with traditional approaches by 3.8 miles, showcasing the depth-based approach as a versatile pre-training technique. Additionally, this study investigates the impact of data augmentation on the depth estimation models.

Complex critical systems necessitate continuous oversight, leading to operator stress and, at times, failure due to an inability to grasp temporal developments within these systems. Current approaches to time-series narration rely on tailored analyses within particular domains, making them impractical for widespread adoption. To address this, we introduce TCube, a universal framework for time-series narration capable of processing diverse domain data, regardless of their nature. TCube employs a transformer-based architecture to generate coherent narratives from temporal time-series information, incorporating an integrated attention mechanism to manage narrative length and prevent irrelevancies. Additionally, TComain-adapters facilitate the adaptation of TCube to various domains through feature extractors that translate time-series data into meaningful concepts. Extensive experiments across six varied domains demonstrate TCube's ability to produce accurate, timely, and relevant, and concise narratives.

The ATLAS experiment has made precise measurements of rare decay probabilities, a key parameter for understanding the weak interaction within beauty mesons, as well as obtained accurate determinations of the angle $\gamma$ associated with CKM unitarity triangle phase differences, through both the ATLAS experiment and previous collaborations involving LHC, Waseda University and Tohoku University.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and examine its interaction through functions. The system's analysis leads to identifying novel periodic and unique states for the Gibbs measure. Additionally, the conditions under which these new weakly periodic states emerge are determined by analyzing the model's ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations.

We investigate a global initial value problem for a first-order system of $m \times m$ linear differential equations, where the coefficients are constrained to be globally sublogarithmic and diverge from the identity matrix at a rate of $1/\ln t$ as $t \to \infty$. The analysis is performed within the framework of an anisotropic Sobolev space, where the time and space variables are treated differently. Under the condition that $s > 1 + m/2$, with $s$ representing the Sobolev space index, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a globally well-posed initial value problem in both the time and space directions.

This paper evaluates the long short-term memory model on the task of Japanese
word segmentation. Given the unique characteristics of Japanese language, such
as the lack of spaces between words and complex segmentation requirements, this
task remains particularly challenging. Recent advancements in Japanese word
segmentation have seen success using both traditional and modern neural network
techniques. Building upon these developments, our research explores the
potential of the long short-term memory model to improve Japanese word
segmentation, achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art models on public
evaluation datasets.

This study investigates the external links frequently shared by Stack Overflow users in their question and answer posts. Despite the potential benefits of enhancing the Platform's relevance and utility, the underlying factors influencing link sharing and the technical barriers to tracking this behavior have not been thoroughly examined. An analysis of data from 2011 to 2021 reveals that a significant proportion of shared links originate from external resources, often promoted by the Stack Overflow community members themselves. Additionally, the research finds that a small fraction of users accounts for the vast majority of shared links, often leading to shared content being rarely accessible at the time of examination. Despite these challenges, the findings suggest that incentive-based models could effectively encourage community members to share more pertinent external resources.

Observations of galaxy properties have reached a point where we can no longer generalize about the typical evolution path of galaxies. This ends the epoch of smooth, monotonic galaxy evolution. Instead, the variations in galaxy properties are now within the limits of measurement tools, making it impossible to separate signals from noise. This challenge, known as the galaxy diversity problem, has been around for some time but now we have enough precise data to test proposed solutions. This paper reviews the most promising solutions to this puzzle. All models attempt to explain how galaxies acquire their properties without fine-tuning. They also show that most of the observed galaxy properties are random. This implies that we don't know much about the true processes at work, even if we can accurately describe how galaxies evolve. This is reminiscent of the "tuning fork" model, which claimed to know how galaxies formed but failed to predict new discoveries. In contrast, the hierarchy model, which uses realistic astrophysical knowledge, acts more like a successful theory like the standard model in particle physics, incorporating multiple effects but struggling to match all observations. Ultimately, this paper suggests that we view galaxy evolution not as following a set path, but as a random process influenced by multiple factors, and that we must be prepared to abandon current models if new data doesn't fit, leading to an unpredictable future in understanding galaxy evolution.

Global climate change communication is hindered by a lack of clarity in the information being conveyed. Although numerous climate experts have been attempting to raise awareness about climate change, there is no single system in place to support them in communicating accurate information. To address this gap, we have developed a Climate Knowledge Base to organize the research findings on climate change, and a Climate Dialogue system that leverages NLP, including the Climate KB, to provide customizable information and recommendations during conversations with climate professionals. This system enhances climate communication by providing supporters with contextual information and relevant research on the user's preferred topic, ultimately facilitating more effective two-way communications.

Clinical symptom extraction from electronic health records is a crucial task for precise extraction, yet it experiences a severe reduction in accuracy when confronted with data from unfamiliar sources. This challenge arises because existing models are specifically tailored to known data sources, limiting their performance on new ones. Citing issues with note structures and language variations across different institutions, their consequences include decreased model effectiveness and potential biases, hindering reliable results for new data sources. This study addresses these issues by introducing SymEvent, a comprehensive dataset comprising 15 million annotated instances and 3.5 million clinical notes from 12 distinct data sources. SymEvent enables the evaluation of extraction performance across multiple data sources and the assessment of domain generalization capabilities, which is critical for real-world applications. Moreover, this research delves into symptom event extraction strategies that rely on the deliberate omission of specific context, unlocking new possibilities for addressing domain adaptation challenges. This new approach, termed Neglect TE, excels over current state-of-the-art benchmarks and showcases promising domain generalization properties, outperforming alternative strategies while achieving exceptional multi-source extraction results on a symmetric benchmark.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods have proven to be a versatile tool for the intricate tasks of autonomous vehicle navigation. Despite its potential, DRL techniques still face several challenges in a wide range of applications, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional and dynamic states. This tutorial addresses a specific DRL problem by using autonomous vehicle navigation as an example. It begins with an introduction to the fundamental concepts of reinforcement learning and deep learning, followed by a detailed explanation of the autonomous vehicle navigation problem, its underlying principles, and existing solutions. The tutorial then introduces deep reinforcement learning, highlighting its advantages and limitations, before presenting a novel framework for solving complex state spaces. This framework integrates deep autoencoders with multiple Q-networks to effectively address and decompose the inherent complexities of the problem.

In recent years, the application of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) has grown rapidly, 
driven by the availability of advanced Hardware Accelerators. Although effective, 
DNNs have a complex structure and a high weight complexity, making them expensive 
to train and operate on standard hardware. To address this issue, researchers proposed 
using Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which offer better neuron and connection complexity 
and adapt well to event-based computing hardware due to their use of difference equations. 
However, the potential of SNNs is limited by existing training algorithms, which are 
often difficult to implement and enhance. This study investigates the use of Stochastic 
Neural Networks (SNNs), incorporating corrected and expanded versions of the Back-Propagated 
Accumulated Error (BPAE) algorithm. To tackle the challenges of traditional Spiking Back-Propagated 
Accumulated Error (SNP), two enhanced versions are introduced: BPAE-SNNSC, which checks the network's 
convergence status, and BPAE-SNNSD, which accelerates the training speed by distributing errors on the network. 
These improvements enable better accuracy, convergence, and rapid error dissemination. 
Experiments demonstrate that the proposed BPAE-SNNSD algorithm outperforms existing methods, 
including BPAE-SNNSC, in terms of accuracy, training time, and energy consumption, 
when using the MNIST

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field and thermal conditions. We analyze the spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of these factors, and derive the equation of state. Additionally, we examine the phase space of spin-polarized strange quark matter as stellar internal parameters vary, in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and in the presence of both spin-polarized and spin-unpolarized muons. Our study also includes an analysis of the pressure profile within these stars, in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and we consider the possibility of observing such objects astronomically.

This research introduces Pando, a personal assistant that collaborates with users to manage digital materials and facilitate meaningful interactions within web browsers. Through a combination of user input and AI-driven knowledge representation, Pando proactively offers relevant suggestions, adapts its recommendations based user preferences, and engages users in dialog to better understand their needs. Furthermore, Pando's capabilities extend to controlling the users digital environment through a conversation-based interface. Conceptually, Pando represents a new direction in assistant-based computing, aiming to support users in accessing digital information and accomplishing personal tasks, ultimately working towards more sophisticated applications like home health and home management.

Relying on the theory of polynomial operator-valued rational interpolation, a novel approach for approximating eigenvalues and eigenvectors of nonlinear matrix problems has been developed. The proposed method involves selecting interpolation points in a rational fashion, with the goal of achieving approximate eigenpairs at points where the approximation error is minimized. The resulting algorithm is efficient, straightforward, and has the advantage of being applicable to any matrix problem, especially in cases with sparse matrices, without incurring additional computational costs. The algorithm features an adaptive strategy for minimizing interpolation error and can be implemented in an efficient way with the SLEPc package. The method's properties, including convergence, have been proven and have been demonstrated in various examples of nonlinear matrix problems.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation, which leaves a specific interval untouched. This equivalence holds under the condition that the set of allowed words in the former system can all be found in the latter, with the added requirement of not containing a specific high-order string with an extended gap. This results in significant implications, with one notable application being the proof that there are uncountably many conjugate intermediate beta-transformations with a specific greedy transformation and fixed gap, provided these transformations satisfy certain conditions. Furthermore, our results reveal that for any given set of allowed words, there are uncountably many intermediate beta-transformations with specific properties, including varying largest return times and words representing these return times.

We've performed an in-depth look at $SO(N_{\textit{c}})$ gauge theories with $N_{\textit{f}}$ pairs of Dirac fermions using lattice regulation, and our results from simulations show that these theories experience confinement. We've found that for both $SO(3)$ and $SO(4)$ cases with $N_{\textit{f}}=2$ pairs, there is distinct disruption of chiral symmetry when the lattice spacing is sufficiently small, which is in line with expectations based on previous research. We've determined that this threshold occurs at a specific, theory-dependent scale and discovered that this threshold can be identified by observing an increase in the step-like pattern of a dimensionless quantity, which is derived from a gauge-invariant loop and depends on the number of colors ($N_{\textit{c}}$) but is independent of the number of fermion pairs. We've found that while there is disruption of chiral symmetry, there is no deconfinement transition up to a high temperature range, which is significantly higher than the scale at which chiral symmetry is disrupted.

Machine learning models like random forests and decision trees are widely used in diverse fields such as finance, biology, and psychology, due to their effectiveness and ability to handle complex data. However, their tendency to create deep models makes their predictions hard to understand, as most of their influence on outcomes is concealed. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces disentangled attribution curves (DACs), a novel method for transparently attributing the impact of data on the predictions made by these algorithms. Unlike traditional explanation techniques that focus on local or global model behavior, DACs provide a granular, instance-specific explanation, offering a detailed view of how data on the training set influenced the model's predictions. In a comparative analysis with alternative attribution techniques, DACs were shown to provide more accurate and consistent results, with initial tests on real-world datasets (finance, biology, and psychology) confirming that using data during training, rather than just on it, leads to more accurate predictions. Consequently, DACs offer valuable insights into the role of in-sample data in the model's development, paving the way for using random forests and decision trees in fields that demand high levels of explanation.

Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized approach to training machine learning (ML) models, keeping data private by preventing it from leaving local sources. Similarly, Multi-Party Computation (MPC), such as in Trusted Computation Platforms (TCPs), secures data and models by preventing them from being disclosed. This research integrates FL and TCPs, specifically kClique and TMVA, to enhance model accuracy and security. A custom FL module was created within the kClique API and tested with the TMVA image classification dataset, with results showing customized functions for both platforms and a functional, albeit resource-intensive (due to increased communication overhead), integration of FL with TCPs.

The complexity of automated driving systems is escalating, incorporating numerous features like high-level path planning, which poses a challenge for testing in real-world scenarios. To address this, we have developed and implemented a scalable solution for collecting and analyzing driving performance data on a a modest embedded system platform. This solution accommodates various driver evaluations, even those on simplified automotive systems, by adapting to different evaluation protocols and contexts. Moreover, our approach integrates a versatile, reconfigurable hardware setup based on the ARM Cortex-A17 processor and a programmable graphics display, providing visual stimuli for testing. This setup proves particularly advantageous for evaluating automated driving performance in technologies that do not necessitate substantial and costly computing resources.

Achieving optimal performance for application platforms and individual software applications necessitates not only efficient development and testing but also effective management of System Call policies across these components. With the advent of containerized microservices, ensuring a secure System Call policy for each microservice has become particularly critical. However, restricting specific System Calls can inadvertently impede their functionality or introduce unexpected disruptions. To address this challenge, we introduce a deep learning-based approach called Timeloops, designed to automatically generate System Call policies for individual microservices within a heterogeneous workload environment. By analyzing the behavior of each microservice through deep Q-learning, Timeloops develops custom System Call policies that not only prevent unauthorized calls but also enhance the efficiency of platform and application metrics, such as cost and response time. Our experimental results demonstrate that Timeloops can successfully train System Call policies for diverse containerized microservices within approximately 5 hours, while accurately preventing unauthorized System Calls and improving performance metrics without restricting specific System Calls.

This research examines linear binary classifiers within different geometric spaces formed by constructing and modifying the standard real Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. By analyzing these classifiers' properties in diverse geometries such as Euclidean, elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic spaces, we provide explicit formulas and investigate their relationships. Additionally, the study extends to examining classifiers within arbitrary Riemannian spaces and linear separators in hyperplanes also known as R-Hyperplanes.

The orbital patterns of stars in the strong gravity area around a central black hole in the Milky Way can be separated into distinct regimes based on the impact of the $\delta$-like potential from the black hole and the more smoothly-varying gravitational effect of the surrounding star cluster. In this paper, the behavior of these orbital patterns changes at the boundary between these regimes, leading to the convergence of calculations from two distinct sets of approximations. A more accurate set of analytical expressions for orbital periods and the precession rates of orbital planes has been developed, which can be used to better understand the orbital patterns of these stars. This new model also takes into account the effects of dark matter, as well as the gravitational influence of the surrounding star cluster and any potential dark matter core.

This work explores the concept of model predictive control beyond linear constraints, delving into the challenges that arise when models are imperfect and when predictions exceed what is computationally feasible. To address these issues, we introduce a probabilistic approach to predictive control, known as random MPC, which leverages predictive distributions to inform control decisions. We evaluate this method in a simulation setting, comparing it to a leading alternative, quasi-opportunistic control, and uncovering that it may prove difficult to implement due to these specific hurdles.

This paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings and algorithmic solutions of the Compressive Singular Evolution Problem (CSEP), a model employed to distill singular components from a matrix of compressed measurements. CSEP is a non-convex optimization problem, and existing solutions rely on alternating minimization methods, leveraging the Rank Minimization Over Sliding Window (RMSW) algorithm to iteratively estimate singular subspaces and evolve them accordingly. However, RMSW is prone to failure in scenarios with low compression rates and the sliding window introduces a limitation, requiring more frequent access to the matrix data. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach that frames access to the matrix as a graph and model the frequency of updates to rows and columns as a traversal, enabling the development of the Singular Component Access Problem (SSEP). We then solve SSEP through an algorithm called SSAP, which we prove converges and surpasses the performance of RMSW in terms of access frequency and optimization results, particularly when employing a graph-based algorithm called MVP to efficiently solve SSAP.

A numerical simulation of a tradeoff between competition and colonization in a math model provides an anatomic explanation for how species coexist after removing species from a population. The model accounts for the competition between two species for resources available at various spatial scales. Depending on the parameters, this tradeoff leads to either the exclusion of one species or the coexistence of both species. The removal of a species from a population corresponds to removing a high-order term from the model's equations, and we investigate how species coexistence is affected by this removal. The numerical results show that removing a species can reveal unstable equilibrium points, and these points can be approached by the species population over time, indicating that the species can coexist even if one species was not present initially.

We examine the endomorphism algebra of the vacuum state in abelian quantum double models, and establish that it coincides with the von Neumann algebra generated by local charges within the respective DHR model. Furthermore, by employing properties specific to the abelian nature of these models, we identify the local von Neumann algebras within the braided category.

We investigate how coherent feedback interacts with a cavity magnomehcnics system and demonstrate that coherent feedback can enhance and sustain tripartite entanglement between magnons, photons, and phonons, as well as stabilize the system's steady state. We utilize the magnitude of logarithmic negativity to assess tripartite entanglement and demonstrate that coherent feedback significantly improves entanglement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that coherent feedback enhances and stabilizes entanglement even under conditions where incoherent feedback fails to do so.

This study presents one-loop approximations for dimensionally-regulated QCD's multiple-collinear parton division triple-collinear splitting operators, with results expressed in a simplified framework. This compilation serves as the basis for calculating virtual corrections to physically possible processes in QCD and novel counterterms needed for next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions in QCD and potential applications in loop massive QCD predictions.

For one-dimensional local rings, the Neron resolution can be replaced with a sequence of rings that maintains the same cohomological characteristics as the original ring, which further simplifies to a dualizing complex in this context. It has been proven that such a resolution exists universally, and more specifically, for Gorenstein rings of prime dimension, the Neron resolution can be substituted with a sequence of modules that forms a finite length complex with perfect homology, which in turn implies the existence of a bounded finite length complex of injective modules with equivalent homology to the ring itself.

The Indonesian archipelago's vast sundial collections are an essential part of the cultural heritage in the Eastern Hemisphere. Historically, sundials were not just timekeeping devices but also symbols of authority for royal and noble families. Due to the lack of a unified time system, each island and region developed its own sundial-based local time. Employing sundials presents unique challenges because of the need to account for geographical locations, varying calendar systems, and the tilt of the Earth. We examine the historical context of Indonesian sundials, exploring their impact on time measurement, local times, and date calculations. The recording of sundials poses difficulties, particularly with legacy instruments, and our research focuses on the Suryakala-Nusantara project, which aims to address these recording issues. The project's timekeeping module is integrated into the main application, which facilitates data entry, timekeeping, and sun position calculations for educational and publishing purposes.

This research paper explores a energy-aware integrated and cooperative D2D communication system, which incorporates a reflectarray, by simulating its thermal emission as a random Gaussian process. A cooperative D2D communication link is set up directly between a user equipment and a D2D user, with their integrated circuit sharing processing, memory, and radio resources. A coordinated reflectarray is strategically placed between this D2D link and the radio frequency source of their integrated circuit. The reflectarray is designed to maximize the energy efficiency of this integrated D2D communication system by carefully adjusting its phase shifts. Specifically, we first use the weighted minimum sum of errors method to formulate an optimized power allocation problem, which then transforms into a standard convex problem. We utilize the interior point method to find an exact solution to this problem. To speed up computation, we introduce a low-complexity beamforming design based on the block coordinate descent approach, which effectively minimizes the beamforming errors. We also present a high-complexity beamforming design that produces a zero sum of errors, which is then simplified into a lower-complexity problem. Finally, the performance of this proposed solution is compared with other alternative solutions under various scenarios.

A proposed conventional single-point LDV system is designed to simultaneously capture x and y velocity components in a two-dimensional space, utilizing a triple-beam arrangement with symmetric configurations. By strategically positioning the triple probes in a Y-shaped setup, this design facilitates the measurement of 2D flows at significant distances, typically around half a meter, by aligning the expansion regions of the probes. For this design to effectively function, it requires precise alignment and symmetry of the triple probes. A suitable computer-based data acquisition system is also essential to operate this setup efficiently. To validate its potential, this LDV-based system was successfully applied to map the velocity profile in a flowing single-phase air environment.

First-order patterns, a logical framework for describing data in databases, have been reinterpreted to accommodate diverse data types and attributes. Previously, the pattern-based approach, first introduced by Duschka and Imbert in 1999, relied on a specific data model with constraints, such as functional dependencies and diversity requirements. This work delves into the complexity of first-order patterns, considering binary relations in addition to functional dependencies, and demonstrates that pattern-based queries are expressible using data-exchange formulations with to-schemas, even under diversity requirements. Furthermore, the authors prove that the data complexity of these queries is either in AC0 or NC2.

The recent introduction of programmable phase plates has greatly improved far-field electron microscopy by facilitating the detection of minute changes in electron wave amplitude. However, a significant limitation remains, primarily stemming from the inability of current programmable phase plates to compensate for electron wavefront distortions caused by defects in optical components within the transmission electron microscope. We introduce a novel programmable phase plate designed to correct aberrations in the electron wavefront and discuss its potential implementation as an add-on module for existing programmable phase plates to expand their functionality.

Our focus is the link between assessment techniques and algorithm efficiency. A case in point is the assessment of search algorithms. We argue that most existing evaluation methods have limited applicability, particularly in the area of binary search. Moreover, we suggest that comparisons should be based on the minimum number of checks required to locate a target or determine its absence. Additionally, we propose that algorithms of limited space consumption should be evaluated using的检查 number with a specific memory constraint. Our analysis encompasses the complete set of possible scenarios and includes the following key findings: Firstly, existing evaluation techniques are often misleading. For instance, average-case analysis suggests that all binary search algorithms have the same efficiency, yet exact analysis reveals significant variations. For example, with a search space size of 100, Algorithm A requires a minimum of 7 checks in its worst-case scenario, while Algorithm B needs at least 8 checks. Our research encompasses all known algorithms as well as any potential algorithms, assuming a specific amount of memory. It's interesting to note that even with unlimited memory, Algorithm B still necessaries at least 8 checks in its worst-case scenario. Moreover, we introduce algorithms that outperform existing algorithms B under specific memory constraints, highlighting both theoretical and practical implications.

We are analyzing a one-dimensional random walk with equal probability of moving left or right, denoted as $S_n$, after $2n$ steps, given that the walk's position is non-negative in all steps up to $n$. In a $d$-dimensional space, we denote the generalized position as a vector $\mathbf{S}_n$, which must have non-zero components in all directions. Our main finding relates the count of valid random walk positions after $n$ steps to values of the Dirichlet series involved. Additionally, we verified our results through direct computation and direct calculation for $L_1$-norm balls in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, which were initially proposed as open questions.

We examine the properties of a polymer black hole model, specifically its central, singular core, viewed from the perspective of its highly redshifted outer regions. These outer regions are effectively at rest relative to a distant observer. Utilizing the 2+2 spacetime symmetry, we isolate the outer horizon as seen by this stationary observer, then apply the loop quantum gravity method to its intrinsic spatial cross-section, resulting in a novel, non-singular, quasi-2D geometry with an intrinsic quantum scale. This approach also yields the black hole's non-trivial quasi-normal mode spectrum, showing the model's agreement with general relativity in the classical limit.

We have developed a comprehensive analytical model for calculating the heat capacity of doped graphene over a wide temperature range. This model incorporates the effects of thermal screening and is expressed in terms of dimensionless variables, thereby simplifying interpretation. What emerges from our research is a previously unidentified physical contribution to the heat capacity, stemming from carriers beyond the Fermi level. Moreover, our findings reveal that thermal screening significantly impacts the heat capacity, leading to distinct behavior in undoped and doped graphs, with undoped graphs exhibiting a non-zero heat capacity as the temperature approaches zero.

Our new system, MaskedSpeech, uses a modified strategy to efficiently combine context information with speech production, overcoming limitations of previous methods that stored extensive contextual data. This novel strategy not only reduces memory consumption but also significantly improves speech quality by ensuring that only relevant context is utilized. Additionally, MaskedSpeech can be training-independent, making it adaptable to various models without altering their original training process. We demonstrate its superiority over the direct concatenation of contextual data and reveal that its performance benefits are consistent across different models and contextual embedding techniques.

We have developed an efficient method that leverages deep learning models to make accurate predictions, particularly when working with limited or unseen data. Deep learning models excel at identifying intricate, underlying patterns in data, but their stochastic nature can pose challenges when used for inference. Current projection predictive methods are designed to utilize trained models for inference by projecting test data into the model's latent space and selecting the most representative training points, thereby enhancing predictive performance. However, our novel variant projects both test data and outcome variables, projecting the latter into the latent space to identify suitable training points, projecting the former to eliminate high-dimensional noise, and ultimately making predictions, all while minimizing the risks of overfitting and test data contamination. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach across various simulation scenarios.

Recent advances in large-scale machine learning have led to remarkable achievements, but they have also opened new avenues for exploitation. Research into how malicious actors can take advantage of machine learning models in a man-in-the-middle scenario is still in its infancy. Our investigation focuses on how such actors can benefit from generative models in a man-in-the-middle attack. Specifically, we show that when an malicious generative model is used as a wrapper around a machine learning classifier, the combined system outperforms traditional attack methods in several tests. Our findings are concerning, especially in scenarios where the malicious generative model is developed without access to the training data of the machine learning classifier being targeted.

Climate change is increasingly being portrayed as a top priority issue by the majority of Americans. However, misinformation about the subject is also spreading rapidly, making it challenging to change people's attitudes toward climate change without first addressing and debunking false claims. A survey of false climate change beliefs circulating on social media among U.S. Facebook users was conducted. The study found that the top misconceptions are related to global temperature trends and the evidence for man-made climate change. Christian fundamentalism, conservatism, and lack of science knowledge are key predictors of climate change misinformation sharing. Surprisingly, formal education and political ideology are not significant predictors. The findings suggest that users with higher conservatism and a lack of science expertise are more likely to engage with climate change misinformation on social media, and that further research is needed to better understand the dynamics at play.

A search for dark matter associated with top quark production is conducted using data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions, comprising a total luminosity of 35.9 fb. The analyzed dataset was obtained from the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The investigated scenarios involve the production of dark matter along with either a top quark or top quark pairs, with the dark matter being assumed to couple to these top quarks through mediators that decay width-relatedly. Six distinct final states are examined, comprising combinations of top quarks and jet configurations resulting from the mediators' visible decay products. The statistical significance of excess events over predicted background events in all final states is maximized at 2.3 standard deviations, with upper limits set on cross-sectional areas at 95% confidence levels. These limits span the ranges of 48 to 910 fb for associated top quark production and 130 to 6100 fb for top quark pair production, depending on the momenta of the mediators and the masses of both the top quarks and mediators.

In this study, we define and investigate the n-extrangement property within a given category, specifically an abelian category with global dimension limited to n or less. We prove that the category of n-extranglements over a self-injective n-extrangement category is also extranglement with respect to the original category and establish that it forms a summand generation of the latter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global dimension of a finite dimensional, simple connected, hereditary quiver representation limit category is exactly n.

This research returns to the foundational work of Heckman and Card on the correlation between student major selection and earnings, a topic Card has been revisiting in his recent studies. Building upon the premise that the decision process for choosing a major is influenced by unobserved factors, Card has argued that standard methods for estimating the effect of a major on earnings may yield biased results due to selection bias. In response, this study challenges Card's key assumption that all major selection interventions can be categorized into distinct groups. By proposing the application of a new statistical approach tailored for such 'mixed' interventions, the authors demonstrate that standard methods using control functions or local regressions can accurately account for selection bias and produce unbiased estimates of the effect of a major on earnings. These findings have important implications not only for the study of the influence of a major on earnings but also for the analysis of other endogenous interventions with multiple choices.

In the early universe, a hypothetical flat, open cosmological model was examined. Initially, such a scenario couldn't be dismissed, largely due to string theory's requirement for 26 dimensions. The most plausible explanation, however, involves a lattice structure where the cosmological model coexists with other lattice elements, such as strings, requiring 26-2026 dimensions to eliminate the mass term's contribution. The most compelling argument stems from quantum mechanics, where the flat, open cosmological model's existence is backed by the simplest wave function possibilities, particularly when initial conditions are perfectly flat.

This paper puts forward a novel approach to the variational segmentation of images, 
integrating the challenges of image denoising, deblurring, deblurring, and decoloration.
The proposed model unites a length-regularized variational method with existing 
image restoration techniques, including total variation and deconvolution methods.
To handle diverse blurring effects, the model employs an adaptive convolutional matrix 
tailored to each case. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new optimization strategy, 
a generalized forward-backward splitting method, enabling the simultaneous 
treatment of convex and smooth components within the model. Experimental results 
validate the efficacy of the proposed variational model in achieving accurate image 
segmentation across various practical scenarios.

Heavy rotating black holes can develop an "hair" when interacting with ultralight particles through a super-radiant process, inhibiting rotation. Researchers have discovered that the spin rates of heavy quasars are largely diminished. By utilizing the lack of hair in these quasars to inhibit the super-radiant instability, scientists can establish a restricted range for the mass of ultralight particles. This restricted range is composed of separate regions, each defined by the quasars with the minimum spin rates.

Our proposed system, the 'Loihi' emulator, enables real-time simulation of neuromorphic algorithms by integrating the Linux kernel and a neuromorphic algorithm compiler, facilitating simple translation of existing algorithms written with the Brian2 simulator. The compiler leverages a customized neuron compiler, utilizing the Clyde simulator to optimize neuron simulation efficiency on Loihi's neural processing unit (NPU) by mapping neuron properties and synapses to the appropriate hardware components (analog or digital). The difference equation emulator (DEE) then applies the selected update rules to all NPUs in parallel, simulating realistic behavior on Loihi.
