Our extensive simulations have shown that Indecision Forests outperform traditional decision trees and other baseline models in terms of accuracy and ability to convey outcome uncertainty through the arguments provided.

The DTW distance is commonly used to calculate the distance between two time series, however its high computational complexity (exponential) makes it impractical for large datasets and real-time applications. A proposed solution is the Early Discarding Pruned DTW, a variation of the DTW algorithm that significantly reduces its computational cost, at the expense of similarity rates. While ED PrunedDTW has made DTW more feasible, its existing implementations still rely on creating a DTW matrix, which hinders its application to large datasets. This paper proposes an alternative implementation of ED PrunedDTW that eliminates the need for the DTW matrix, making it applicable to large datasets and real-time applications. The proposed implementation uses search techniques to find the DTW distance at specific points, which only requires the time series and no additional data structures. By avoiding the creation of data structures, this new implementation minimizes memory usage and makes search possible. The paper demonstrates the feasibility of using the new ED PrunedDTW implementation on large datasets and provides experimental results on its performance, including the use of indexing for efficient similarity search.

In software testing education, instructors face a significant obstacle in determining the most effective methods to convey feedback to students about their test cases. An experiment is conducted to compare the effectiveness of inquiry-based conceptual feedback with traditional comprehensive feedback in teaching software testing, yielding the following findings. When students receive inquiry-based conceptual feedback, they demonstrate higher proficiency in understanding the feedback and applying it correctly. Furthermore, this type of feedback leads to improved academic performance and reduces dependency on instructor guidance. On the other hand, while traditional thorough feedback yields better performance overall, the difference becomes insignificant in the later stages. Ultimately, this research suggests that traditional thorough feedback might be more suitable for introductory topics, while inquiry-based conceptual feedback might be more appropriate for advanced topics.

In the exorbitant financial losses incurred by self-driving cars due to their inability to explain accidents, the need for transparent and interpretable AI has become increasingly critical. The field of Explainable AI is expanding to incorporate this urgency. However, explaining the decisions made by state-of-the-art machine learning models like deep neural networks remains a significant challenge owing to their inherent complexity. By combining the strengths of concept analysis and inductive logic programming, we propose a novel approach, called in concept the inductive logic programming model (ILAC), which can effectively define the reasons behind a DNN's predictions on the test set with a concept analysis procedure. Furthermore, our method, the ILAC, can define complex, intangible, and expressive explanations by integrating logical reasoning and intrinsic model features, which are extracted using the concept analysis algorithm. The individual components of this model, a logical rule and a concept definition, can be universally applied to a DNN's predictions on individual input samples and future instances, respectively. In a series of comprehensive numerical evaluations, we showcase that the ILAC defines more granular and conceptually understandable explanations with a predictive accuracy that matches or surpasses existing inductive methods.

One promising neural network model for generating high-quality image colors from grayscale inputs is the graph convolutional network (GCN). However, the over-blurring phenomenon in GCN-based methods leads to inaccurate color generation. To address this issue, we introduce the over-blurring regularization (OBR) that minimizes the differences between the original and denoised color images, thereby mitigating over-blurring. Experimental results demonstrate that O-enhanced GCN produces substantially more vivid and diverse colors. Additionally, the four levels of OBR regularization are found to be more effective than the OBR alone in combating over-blurring.

Researchers conducted a search for dark matter associated with a leptonically decaying Z boson within proton-proton collisions. The experiment, carried out using the CMS detector at the CERN LHC and analyzing 137 nb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, expected the dark matter to be produced along with the Z boson, resulting in events containing two charged leptons and signs of missing transverse momentum. The data was analyzed with various control samples in order to restrict the background from standard model processes. The results did not surpass the sensitivity of the experiment, leading to the establishment of 95% confidence level limits on the cross-sectional areas and dark matter model parameters for three distinct models. The findings further imposed constraints on the interaction between the dark matter particles and quarks, limiting the cross-sectional interaction between a 10 GeV dark matter particle and electrons or quarks to values of 2.6 x 10^-40 cm^2 and 1.6 x 10^-38 cm^2, respectively.

We've developed new models for particle distributions that incorporate transverse momentum, providing a more accurate representation of data from particle collisions compared to the existing Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein models. These updated distribution functions incorporate a function that relates to the spatial distribution of particles within the quark, essentially mirroring how mass influences particle interactions. By combining this model with the typical thermal energy term, our proposed distributions better align with actual particle collision outcomes. Furthermore, we derived expressions for the average energy and energy density that include spatial and transverse momentum effects, showing that our model better represents particle collision data than the standard models.

Any space with a specific type of structure allows for the creation of a corresponding topological group, making topological groups a specific type of space with a special type of clothing, known as 'stockings'. We've discovered the exact conditions under which long colimits of topological groups can be calculated, which allows us to prove that this subgroup, known as G, is actually equal to the sum of the groups involved in the diagram plus a type of free group built on the homologies of the diagram's nerves. We've developed a way to calculate 'free' topological groups using our understanding of these conditions, which ultimately reveals that groups with a certain type of structure, known as ANRs, have properties that make their free groups relatively easy to understand.

The advancement of Heusler technology relies on refined production techniques for high-quality materials, which our research focuses on. Specifically, we investigate how to influence the structural properties and lattice mismatches of MnPt layers through various deposition methods, such as remote epitaxy on graphene, direct deposition with a buffer layer, and direct deposition on a substrate with a large lattice mismatch. By utilizing remote epitaxy on graphene substrates, we discover that thin MnPt layers develop a specific crystalline structure and exhibit a unique orientation with a distinct preference for a certain plane. Furthermore, our findings reveal that this method can compensate for large lattice mismatches, and the epitaxial relationship between MnPt and graphene can be maintained when transitioning to thicker films that exhibit a different phase with a preferred orientation on the substrate. In contrast, direct deposition of MnPt onto the substrate with a large lattice mismatch results in a specific crystalline structure with distinct morphological features, while the addition of a buffer layer yields films with improved structural properties and a unique orientation with a preferred plane. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the choice of deposition method and underlying substrate can significantly influence the phase formation and orientation of Heusler layers, and these findings contribute to the advancement of the Heusler technology.

We analyze long sequences of multivariate data, assuming the underlying process is a mixture of two distinct regimes, one characterized by light tails and the other by heavy tails, as seen in financial markets. This behavior is captured using regime-switching Gaussian models. The coexistence of these opposing tail characteristics poses significant challenges for model selection and parameter estimation. To address these challenges, we develop models with flexible mean and covariance structures, and design novel inference methods capable of identifying the regime switching pattern, along with the tail regimes, in multivariate time series data. The effectiveness of our proposed methods is showcased through simulations and applied to a study of S\&P 500 component returns from 1991 to 2021.

Recent JWST observations of distant galaxy clusters have yielded significant results, including the discovery of numerous high-redshift objects. However, these findings require accurate lens modeling to correctly interpret the results. A recently discovered and massive galaxy cluster, located at a redshift of 0.54, utilized the lensing effect to magnify and reveal multiple galaxy formations at greater distances. This lens model, refined by incorporating data from JWST observations, included a precise description of a particular arc, which exhibited multiple images of a galaxy at a redshift of 0.71. These observations provided valuable data for understanding the distribution of matter in the universe. Analysis revealed two noteworthy findings: Firstly, a clump of dark matter situated at a radius of approximately 2.6 kiloparsecs, which is denser and located further from the center than predicted by the standard model. Secondly, the discovery of a object with a redshift of 0.16, which is situated behind the cluster and exhibits a lensed image. This object, which is identified as a red supergiant star, represents the farthest red supergiant discovered in space. By incorporating data from JWST into the lens model, researchers have been able to accurately predict the location and density of this secondary arc, which was confirmed by the JWST observations. This model provides crucial information for understanding the distribution of dark matter in the universe and the evolution of galaxies over time.

A recurring issue in the internet industry is the disparity in quality of service between content and service providers, often due to the latter's lack of incentive to invest in infrastructure. This letter aims to resolve such differences by proposing a profit-sharing agreement between a content provider and a service provider. Under this arrangement, the service provider increases its revenue through improved quality of experience, leading to higher subscription profits and increased quality of service ratings from the content provider. The negotiations between the two parties are modeled as a Stackelberg game, with the content provider acting as the leader and the service provider as the follower. The analysis reveals a unique Nash equilibrium in the best-response game between the parties, which in turn leads to a Stackelberg equilibrium. Computational examples validate the effectiveness of the profit-sharing agreement in achieving a win-win scenario for both providers.

In physics, particularly in quantum theory, the construction of a Hilbert space is crucial. We demonstrate that the methods used by Massey, Murray, Naidu, and Mielke, Muckenheim, Obukhov, and Popov, as well as the approaches of Zhai, Su, and Wang, to derive the Hilbert space from a classical set of observables and states, can be more closely related through their use of 2-categorical techniques. This relationship shows that the authors' methods are essentially equivalent, a conclusion supported by similar earlier work of Mielke and Popov. Furthermore, the authors' equivalence leads to a notable consequence: the recovery of the quantum Hilbert space from a classical set of observables and states always results in a Hilbert space, a property that may be seen as an algebraic version of the Wigner-Holomorph theorem.

The maximum of the scalar field's potential in $\alpha$-attractor models reaches its peak value, $v$, times $3+2\alpha$ times the square root of $(1+2\alpha)$. This peak determines the ultimate density parameter in these models. We've developed the most general $\alpha$-attractor cosmology that starts with a scalar field, then evolved into a cosmological constant through an exponential function. We've studied how long the scalar field lasts, how long the scalar field's rolling motion lasts, and how the cosmological constant's horizon size evolves. We also derived the peak potential in this specific model and found the peak occurs at zero when $\alpha$ approaches zero, but shifts to a positive value as $\alpha$ increases. This peak occurs just outside the scalar field's deconfined region, indicating a nearly flat potential at the peak. The peak occurs when the scalar field's energy density equals the cosmic background radiation, resulting in a predicted peak value close to $v\times 3+2\alpha\times\sqrt{(1+2\alpha)}$. This peak value is predicted to be close to the peak value in natural supergravity models. The predicted peak value is independent of the scalar field's initial placement, resulting in a predicted peak value close to the peak value in natural supergravity models. In our investigation, we examine whether Benzecri's conjecture holds for certain types of hyperbolic three-dimensional manifolds. Specifically, we focus on manifestly hyperbolic manifolds whose isometry groups consist of two disjoint collections of circular regions. These regions interact with the manifold's hyperbolic structure to create complex, measured foliations that extend to its infinite extent. The key question is whether these geometric components remain consistent across all possible quasi-Fuchsian manifolds. Our study reveals that this consistency is not universally true, but it does seem to hold in certain close proximity to a special subset of these manifolds, characterized by a particularly symmetric and real-valued structure.

This paper introduces a new approach called PCR (return cross-sectional allocation) to measure how portfolio returns are distributed across securities within a portfolio, providing an alternative to the common longitudinal allocation focus. Research indicates that the long-term changes in a portfolio's returns may be driven more by shifts in the returns of individual securities rather than the overall portfolio structure. PCR is P's (R1-R2...)(R1-R2...)(R1...R2...), where the terms in brackets represent the returns of securities at different times, and P can range from -infinity to +infinity, and is calculated using the cross-sectional deviations from the mean return. Utilizing real-world data from mutual funds and a comprehensive database of US stock returns, the study demonstrates the mean return deviation from the mean security return can account for a substantial portion of a portfolio's total return. Utilizing a regression analysis that incorporates the model-based allocation returns, the results show that the mean deviation from the mean return explains a substantial portion of a portfolio's total return. Utilizing a theoretical and practical analysis, the study offers insights into the relationship between the returns of individual securities within a portfolio, and how this relationship can be used to explain a portfolio's total return. Utilizing an expanded database, the results show that the mean deviation from the mean return explains up to 40% of a portfolio's total return. Early detection of heart defects and disorders via auscultation has historical significance, yet current methods fall short of identifying abnormal heart sounds in clinical settings. This study addresses the challenge of heart sound categorization under noisy conditions, comparing the performance of Magnitude-Average (MAGN) and Magnitude-Angle (MAGNA) filters in mitigating various types of additive noise, including muscle noises and others. The comparative analysis of the two filters reveals that MAGN exhibits superior noise-eliminating capabilities. Following the denoising process, the manuscript presents a novel deep learning architecture, based on a Cardiac Phonocardiogram ConvNet model, for accurate heart sound classification, addressing issues related to data imbalance, signal distortion, variable signal lengths, and class imbalance. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, achieving accurate categorization of heart sounds in datasets with high noise levels (20 dB).
In this response, we address and respond to the commentary published in Physical Review Letters by Sotnikov et al.

A twist operator functioned as a twist field at its core, marking the beginning of conformal field theory's development decades ago. It was discovered that inserting twist operators into conformal field theory correlation functions is akin to creating an R-manifold, a technique particularly beneficial in string theory, where it facilitated the construction of orientables. Our investigation involves conformal field theory and string theory on the torus, focusing on twist operators that correspond to the diverse 2-D crystallographic point groups within the framework of the GSO projection. We derived explicit formulas for the crystallographic twists on the torus amplitudes, analyzing their symmetrical properties in detail. We examined the role of R-manifolds in this context, investigating their topological characteristics, especially where the twist operators are located on the torus. Our analysis also encompasses Fermions, Bosonized Fermions, and Elliptic Generators, and we discuss the amplitudes of orientables in K3 surfaces and Mirror Symmetry.

A two-sector economic model is examined in an infinite-horizon, stochastic environment with uncertain weather conditions. The environment features overlapping generations and weather influences both production and personal consumption climate. The study derives first-order conditions, and then, under specific assumptions, it's demonstrated that the consumption climate has a positive correlation with the environment's state. Furthermore, the consumption climate exhibits oscillations around its long-term average. The model also shows the existence of unique long-run equilibrium values, and the consumption climate converges towards this equilibrium over time as generations change. The consumption climate's volatility is found to be inversely proportional to the number of generations. The study also analyzes how a more cohesive community impacts optimal consumption and investment strategies.

This research paper develops a framework for handling infinite series of discrete fractional operators, specifically focusing on the properties of $H^p$-boundedness for p ranging from the dimension of the space plus 1 up to infinity. The paper's investigation into Hardy spaces is driven by the need to study the Lefschetz properties of the Riemann surface of the Gamma function. The paper's findings confirm the convergence of Nevanlinna's expansion for any discrete fractional operator and demonstrate the existence of a unique lifting operator from $H^p$ to the space of $L^p$ functions. Additionally, the paper's operator-based approach provides novel proofs for the Lefschetz properties, along with the strong Lefschetz properties at the boundary, thereby resolving the Lefschetz distribution theorem in the context of $H^p$.

Recent research suggests that humans frequently deviate from standard rational assumptions, especially in second-price auctions, where many participants tend to value items based on their own valuations rather than the highest competing bid. We conducted a test of this behavior in second-price auctions with known outcomes, excluding any influence from post-auction feedback. Results show a considerable level of non-rational decision-making, with factors such as participant's initial valuation, the anticipated winning bid, and previous experience all playing a role in how participants value a second-price auction item. We developed a model that accurately predicts participants' bidding strategies and demonstrated its superiority over traditional rational models. Furthermore, we found that our model is resilient to changes in auction settings, suggesting a degree of consistency in our estimates.

The mechanism by which the universe's isotropy is achieved holds significant importance, and we investigate this phenomenon within the framework of the locally rotationally symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I model under Q-gravity theory. This novel approach leads to three distinct scenarios that facilitate the universe's isotropization. Moreover, we study various cosmological parameters by considering both anisotropic and isotropic dynamics. The resulting data indicate that Q-gravity theory effectively explains the universe's expansion history. Additionally, we examine how Q-gravity resolves the over-density problem associated with the standard Lambda-CMD model, and we compare the fit between these theories and the dataset provided by Planck 2013.

We develop a new geometric algorithm for resolving singularities of algebraic varieties, extending the combinatorial vertex decomposition of intersection ideals to the geometric setting. This method produces a chain of resolutions, linked with a Gröbner basis and a Frobenius partition in characteristic $p > 0$. We apply this algorithm to Hessenberg varieties for a regular nilpotent element and demonstrate that the resulting minimal model is a sequence of smooth Hessenberg varieties. Furthermore, we discover a connection between our algorithm and the iterative structure of the Hessenberg varieties themselves.

Neural Painters, an autonomous agent, generates brushstrokes for a given image, enabling exploration of a network as a stochastic process. As GPON progresses, brushstrokes are created from random noise, allowing a step-by-step generation of the final image. We have assessed GPON's capabilities as a generative model on synthetic Delight images, demonstrating its ability to recreate the original image after a specified number of steps. Furthermore, GPON's generative process enables the creation of novel Delight-like images by choosing a step count that reveals pleasing, coherant images. By randomizing operator and operand choices for each step, GPON can generate "hallucinated" images that may deviate from the original after a certain step count. We've applied GPON to popular popular networks ResNet and ShakeNet, achieving a low reconstruction error of around 0.050 ± 0.002 on the ImageNet database. We've also demonstrated GPON's capacity as a generative model by producing art-acceptable images at a coarse scale and explored its potential for visualisation by training on the Delight dataset.

The presence of anomalous patterns in the decay rates of B-mesons can be attributed to new physics phenomena. Specifically, a distinctive pattern in leptonic decays is observed, while flavor-changing effects are seen in both neutral and charged current processes. This anomalous pattern can be naturally explained by a model involving composite, vector-like particles, which also modify the dipole moments of particles. This explains a specific relationship between different decay rates: $R_{D^{(*)}}/R_{K^{(*)}} \approx 1.5$. Furthermore, by analyzing the di-Higgs production rate in gluon fusion, we can constrain the scale of these composite particles, which should be above 1.5 TeV based on recent measurements at the Large Hadron Collider.

We present a unique dataset known as QuoraRA, which comprises interaction data from the Quora platform. QuoraRA includes questions and answers based on research papers, specifically those asking for knowledge not found in the papers but supported by external knowledge sources. Based on user feedback, we aim to support authors in gathering necessary information during reading research papers. To this end, we developed a task called Knowledge-Seeking Question Answering (KSQA). By examining how KSQA differs from existing tasks, such as Reading Comprehension and Question Generation, we investigate the uniqueness of the KSQA task. To analyze the sources that KSQA answerers rely on, we conducted an experiment called Labelled Data Source Extraction (LDASE). To facilitate KSQA's integration into Reading Comprehension and Reading Comprehension-based Question Generation, we conducted two experiments named Adaption to RCQA and Adaption to RQG. The results of these experiments led us to conclude that KSQA possesses distinct characteristics not found in existing tasks and that current models do not excel at answering KSQA questions. Nevertheless, we found that a model specially designed for KSQA outperforms general-purpose quora reading comprehension and question generation models, but surprisingly struggles to compete with large language models such as GPT-3.

In three-dimensional core-collapse supernovae models, fast neutrino flavor instabilities originate in the regions where the core is recoiling. These regions are predominantly present when the core collapse is initiated. The instability tends to avoid dense knots. As the models progress, the instability primarily affects neutrinos. Its presence is often associated with the proto-neutron star oscillations. The instability's impact can cause irregularities in the neutrino energy spectra. It may result in the development of multiple muon neutrino clusters. The instability may erthe the proto-neutron star, causing the star to lose energy. This impact can impact the supernova process. Moreover, the instability may trigger or intensify convection patterns, influencing the development of the proto-neutron star. Understanding and researching these phenomena is crucial for gaining insights into the complex inner workings of supernovae.

ADHD is a widely prevalent neurodevelopmental issue that extends into multiple aspects of a person's life. Utilizing structural MRI and rs-fMRI data, we've been attempting to identify a brain-based classification model for ADHD. Leveraging the vast richness of MRI data has led to the application of deep learning, despite its challenge of requiring the entire brain as input. Our goal is to pinpoint a critical brain region for ADHD using rs-fMRI's intrinsic connectivity, thereby reducing the input required for our model. To achieve this, we've developed an intrinsic connectivity metric by analyzing rs-fMRI's temporal patterns, then used Geneski's intrinsic time series expansion to identify connectomes, applying Geneski's intrinsic decoherence time criterion to filter out noise. Next, we've utilized the intrinsic and orthogonal triangularization method to extract critical brain regions from the reduced connectomes. By applying our framework to both rs-fMRI and structural MRI data, we've found that an input of 22 components can achieve superior ADHD classification performance compared to the full model. Our findings align with prior MRI-based studies of ADHD and highlight a brain-based classification model using a significantly reduced input.

Over recent years, computer security modeling through discrete-time Markov processes 
has gained significant attention.  This paper presents a new SISI model, designed to 
simulate outbreaks in a network, and uses matrix theory to analyze its properties. 
Specifically, we examine the model's non-extinction, extinction, and stationary 
distributions.  Our results are then applied to investigate the long-term behavior 
of the system as well as the impact of preventing infected systems from transmitting 
data to other nodes.  To support our findings, simulations are presented.

Automatically identifying and clarifying the meaning of abbreviations in text is a difficult task for natural language processing systems, particularly when dealing with frequently used short forms. A more complex issue arises when short forms are encountered for the first time, as their meaning cannot be inferred from prior knowledge. This can lead to challenges in determining the underlying full-form words. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach called MadDog, which leverages a graph-based method to relate short forms to their potential meanings, incorporating additional knowledge from social media and employing machine learning to improve its effectiveness. Moreover, our system can handle new and previously unseen short forms, incorporating their meaning into its knowledge base for future use. The madDog web platform not only demonstrates our algorithm but also serves as a reference tool, offering a comprehensive database of established short form relationships, along with a user-friendly interface to contribute new discoveries and customize the graph with personal knowledge.

A key factor in determining the behavior of quantum hall junctions is the difference in thermal conductance between the right and left leads. This leads to the development of nonreciprocal thermal electric (TE) properties. Firstly, it enables the reversible switching of TE conversion direction by adjusting the interference patterns in leads through magnetic modulation. This switchiness arises from the cross interference between the right and left leads. Secondly, based on the key influence of lead asymmetry, it is possible to create heat rectification functionality within the junctions, resulting in non-linear relationships between heat and electrical currents.

DNA-based storage systems take advantage of the high-density properties of DNA and the parallel processing capabilities of the access approach to store data using a parallel and stateless access method. However, this paper recognizes a critical limitation of existing DNA-based storage systems: their inability to accommodate the hierarchical nature of most modern binary files. In addition, their unidirectional access approach makes it difficult to update or delete arbitrary portions of the stored data. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a novel DNA-based storage scheme called DXS. The proposed scheme leverages LDPC codes and coding strategies, including truncation and shortening, along with error correction techniques, like the syndrome decoders. These concepts effectively address the issues of data updates and arbitrary data access in DNA-based storage systems, leading to superior performance in terms of lower error rates and higher data capacity. The effectiveness of the proposed scheme is demonstrated through numerical analysis and simulations.

Topological insulators represent a promising class of materials characterized by exceptional properties of spin-momentum locked surface states, exhibiting remarkable transport phenomena such as the quantum Hall effect without Landau levels and dissipationless thermoelectric responses. While significant progress has been made in understanding the underlying physics of topological materials formed by electron spins, nascent research has centered on exploiting nodal line spectra in topological constants located in momentum space, manifesting as Dirac or Weyl points. This review aims to summarize recent advancements of nodal lines in momentum space, as seen in various systems such as Dirac and Weyl semimetals, and their realization in different materials and photonic systems. Moreover, it explores the relationship between topological nodal lines and other forms of topological singularities, discussing the implications of such connections on topological constants and realizations in different systems.

We examine the movement speed of oscillation patterns in a two-dimensional critical gel phase of the FitzHugh-Nagumo model. This model is used to simulate biological firing mechanisms in neurons. In aligned with prior research by Redondo and Muratore-Ginanneschi (2014), our analysis of parameter space reveals two distinct regimes. In the first regime, our results show a correlation with the parameter $a$ and follow the relationship $v \sim a^{1/2}$. This is comparable to the eikonal approach, which yields the same dependence on the parameter $a$ but differs in its dependence on the other parameter, $b$. Conversely, in the second regime, our results indicate a relationship with the parameter $b$ described by $v \sim b^{2/3}$. The established comparisons with existing literature provide a better understanding of the results and offer a better context for further investigation.

A fundamental concept, the quantum entropy of a state, determines essential characteristics of composite quantum systems. Currently, calculating it exactly requires a full knowledge of the system's underlying state, which is often impractical for unknown quantum systems as measurement precision increases linearly with the system size. A new approach presents a way to estimate quantum entropy from $O(\sqrt[N]{m})$ measurements of $m$ basis elements, where $m$ scales as $2^{O(\sqrt{N})}$ and $N$ denotes the system's total size. Moreover, a scheme exists for estimating entropy with $O(\text{poly}(\kappa,\epsilon)^{\sqrt{N}})$ measurements, where $\kappa$ represents a confidence parameter and $\epsilon$ represents an error parameter. Furthermore, we introduce a method for estimating entropy with high accuracy and confidence using a number of measurements proportional to $\frac{\log\epsilon}{\epsilon^2}$. A new method also enables the extraction of additional information from measurements used to estimate entropy, allowing for the joint estimation of entropy and support size, with the number of measurements scaling as $O(\sqrt[N]{m})$, where $m$ is the sum of the exponential terms based on the entropy and support size.

The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), technology, and engineering is characterized by distinct technical considerations specific to AI algorithms and intelligence applications. AI technical factors pertain to distinctive technologies, architectures, and technical protocols used in AI development, encompassing elements such as data storage, cloud infrastructure, and pipeline management. These technical factors, while essential for AI technical operations, are separate from business goals and objectives. Despite comprising non-strategic elements, AI technical factors play a significant role in shaping an organization's AI technical capabilities and can influence its AI technical strategy. Consequently, they warrant increased attention from AI technical strategists and engineers. This paper explores the definition and significance of AI technical factors within the context of data storage, cloud infrastructure, and AI pipeline management. It emphasizes the need to distinguish between AI technical and nontechnical factors to clarify the scope and boundaries of AI strategic planning. Additionally, the paper highlights the need to develop new frameworks and tools to effectively manage and optimize these technical considerations to enhance overall AI technical efficiency and support data storage, cloud infrastructure, and pipeline management more broadly.

This study proposes an innovative, semi-self-supervised approach for automatically identifying International Classification of Diseases in electronic medical records. Our method leverages ICD codes from prior years as a resource to improve models trained on specific disease categories, eliminating the need for meticulously crafted rules. Instead, we employ a generic framework capable of adapting to various diseases with minimal adjustments. Our experiments demonstrate that the semi-self-supervised approach outperforms supervised models and shows significant year-to-year consistency in performance. Moreover, we find that the additional benefit from adapting to new classes on different years to be substantial and is influenced by feature overlap between ICD codes within and across diseases. This evaluation highlights the potential of semi-self-supervised methods for efficient model development in clinical settings.

A monomial ideal $I$ in a polynomial ring $S$ is considered nearly Cohen-Macaulay when the quotient $S/I$ has local cohomology modules with specific characteristics, particularly for a height of $I$ equal to one less than $S$.

Recent advancements in quantum computing have led to the development of sophisticated quantum machine learning algorithms, which outperform their classical counterparts in various scenarios. These algorithms, although complex to implement due to the challenges associated with quantum states, have become feasible with the emergence of sophisticated quantum computing machines. This study demonstrates the implementation and execution of state-of-the-art quantum neural networks on superconducting processors, yielding significant performance improvements. Moreover, a novel quantum dimension reduction technique, previously impossible to implement, has been successfully realized, leading to substantial benefits. Additionally, the study explores the effects of various quantum properties on unsupervised learning, givings insights into the beneficial potential of quantum computing. These findings have facilitated the development of a wide range of quantum computing-based applications, encompassing the design of quantum-enhanced models with compact circuit structures. Ultimately, the results present a pathway towards the implementation of quantum neural networks on existing quantum computing hardware.

The KMTNet3 planet-hosting catalog is undergoing updates following a comprehensive review of data from the 2018 observation seasons, expanding the collection to 119 confirmed exoplanets, notably incorporating 87 microlensing anomalies discovered by KMTNet's T2 telescope. Our 2018-prime field analysis represents the initial incorporation of KMTNet's S2 and S3 operations, as well as subsequent updates, aiming to provide a thorough understanding of these phenomena. The revised collection is accessible online at exoplanetcatalog.kmt.net, complemented by KMTNet's full-prime field and differential-prime field collections, as well as the underlying raw data at https://github.com/leejeongyeol12345/2018-prime and https://github.com/leejeongyeol12345/d-2018-prime.

A crucial component in solving inverse problems via gradient descent is access to shadow data, specifically the gradient of the loss with respect to model parameters. Traditionally, this is either approximated via finite differences or precisely calculated but at a high computational cost using adjoint methods. In this research, we develop a gradient backprojection technique that not only determines exact gradients but also does so efficiently and differentially. Our approach leverages the structure of linear systems to obtain backprojection operators from pre-solved forward and adjacency systems, requiring the solution of two additional sets of equations solely for shadow computation. Additionally, we propose an iterative method to reuse solutions of these systems across consecutive network layers, significantly lowering the computational burden. The efficacy of our approach is validated through experiments on shadow image restoration, shading removal, and image deblurring, showcasing substantial computational time reductions without compromising performance.

This paper develops a statistical inference framework for dynamic transport demand models by applying maximum a posteriori estimation and empirical bayesian methods to observed traffic patterns. The approach leverages daily travel data between origin-destination pairs to estimate the distribution of traffic flow patterns, without making assumptions about their probability distribution. The method is illustrated through applications using real-world data, with no preconditions on the underlying distribution. Furthermore, the framework enables evaluation of the origin-destination demand matrix on specific routes by analyzing the estimated posterior distribution. The study is grounded in moderate asymptotic theory and relies on direct data analysis for reliable inference.

The behavior of an oscillator array, whose组成 and interaction strengths vary randomly, was examined in an algebraic model where each unit's oscillation strength and mutual interaction strengths are heterogeneous. The results show that these arrays exhibit more than two distinct types of synchronization dynamics. The specific conditions for each type of synchronization, low, medium, and low-robustness synchronization, are derived using linear stability analysis and remain consistent across various degrees of heterogeneity. Furthermore, a scenario where medium-robustness synchronization transforms into low-robustness synchronization was also identified. The current findings provide an essential theoretical foundation for understanding complex neural networks with varying properties.

In 2018, a short proof was provided that the distribution of Aldous-Broder's random walk algorithm on an arbitrary finite graph G is equivalent to Wilson's random loop-erased algorithm, generating a sample from the distribution of uniform spanning trees. However, this equivalence holds solely for the final algorithm snapshot and does not imply that Wilson's and Aldous-Broder's approaches are mutually convertible throughout their execution. Moreover, two distinct issues arose from this finding: Firstly, generating a sample from the uniform spanning tree distribution using Aldous-Broder's approach demands the creation of the entire tree, hindering memory efficiency. Secondly, the acceptance of every walk in Aldous-Broder's process results in a suboptimal O(mn) time complexity, leading to a dual problem where unnecessary and unerasable loops are removed. We have rectified these drawbacks by demonstrating that G's structure allows high probabilities of creating only essential and then a second, memory-efficient and time-optimized (at least as fast as Wilson's approach) algorithm involving two stages.

This paper presents a novel dataset known as MusicTM-Dataset, which is a pioneering collection that integrates sheet music, lyrics, and recorded music, enhancing it with additional metadata. Complementing the dataset is the proposed sheet music encoder, which leverages a transformer architecture to process musical notation directly in vector space by decoding musical symbols using contextual clues. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to previous methods and other baseline models on two existing music-related tasks, two common benchmarks. Finally, two new tasks have been created and achieved impressive results, specifically in sheet music retrieval and sheet music re-ranking for music retrieval tasks.

This research paper examines how word embeddings can enhance visual data exploration tools like Ontodia, a semantic web ontology editor and visualizer. By applying machine learning techniques to large, structured data sets, such as Wikidata, we can identify latent connections between data entities and represent them in a form that can be visually analyzed for patterns. In collaboration with Ontodia, our development aims to apply word embedding analysis to the top 10,000 most frequently accessed Wikidata items, mapping their properties and values to create a graph that can be visually explored and interactively studied.

The influence of an optical management technique, which modifies dispersion based on intensity, on dark solitons in one-dimensional systems is investigated. Numerical simulations of the Schrödinger equation reveal that, for systems with negative dispersion, dark solitons remain stable and exhibit a shrinking gap. The long-term stability of the dark soliton is confirmed, which contrasts with the results obtained in previous studies that assumed uniform dispersion. However, it is found that bright and dark-bright solitons remain unstable under these conditions.

This paper explores the concept of structured guidance in visual analytics to assist analysts in navigating complex processes. Through an in-depth review of existing research and theoretical frameworks, we introduce Lotse, a practical architecture designed to facilitate guided interactions during comprehensive visual analytics investigations. We illustrate Lotse's effectiveness with a case study utilizing great apes genomic data, and subsequently evaluate its suitability, as well as identify areas for future improvement, based on this case study.

Magnetic confinement, a key aspect of nuclear fusion research, utilizes the Frensley stellarator to trap hot plasma within tokamaks and other devices employing a twisted magnetic field. To facilitate fusion research and development, advanced computational tools such as NIPE and MOOSE/Notebook have been utilized to design and optimize the Next Generation Torus (NGT) magnetic coil system. Through careful analysis, we have discovered that an initially developed 36-coil NGT magnetic system is robust against external disturbances and maintains stable plasma confinement. Furthermore, this magnetic system can adapt to various scenarios, including tokamak operations with external coils disabled and steady-state plasma scenarios utilizing non-inductive current drive.

Temperature variations within fixed beds of particles are being studied using an advanced technique, rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in combination with a specific contrast agent. A gas-solid system is quickly temperature-tested after being introduced in a rapid MRI-compatible column. The temperature is first assessed at two starting points: uniform and random initial temperatures for the particles, and a high temperature for the bed itself. These initial conditions are then monitored as the bed settles due to gravity and as a solid flow moves through it during rapid gravity filling and quick-seal operations. Temperature fluctuations during the settling and quick-seal processes are captured and analyzed using 3D-MRI temperature maps. Results reveal non-uniform temperature patterns at the bed surface when particles settle and solidify, and distinct temperature profiles emerge with the progression of the solid flow front. Specifically, random initial temperatures lead to lower temperatures at the bed surface, while uniform initial temperatures result in higher temperatures. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of rapid MRI in measuring temperature variations within fixed beds of particles and provides valuable insights for understanding solidification and fluidization processes.

To understand the behavior of multiple growing entities with interacting components, we investigated a model where elliptical aggregates form through the addition and removal of components from their perimeters, which occur with probabilities inversely related to their sizes. We examined how this process plays out in systems containing complementary shapes that attract each other and in which only one shape type is initially present, leading to the discovery that the initial structure can influence final outcomes with two main results emerging: (a) only one shape type remains stable, or (b) both shape types coexist in a stable state.

Our study focused on examining the behavior of magnetic fields within two major sunspots, denoted as $\delta$-sunspots, that were part of a solar active region observed by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope. These $\delta$-sunspots exhibited an unusual and rapid rotation, and we found that their magnetic fields underwent a significant reconfiguration due to forces exerted by coronal material. This $\delta$-sunspots rotation, which previously had not been seen, may be associated with sub-eruptions that occurred near the active region, and we found evidence for the presence of microflares that could have influenced the rotation process. Furthermore, our analysis revealed another magnetic disturbance within one of the sunspots that caused the sunspot to shift position and caused the detection of another sub-eruption. This suggests that the $\delta$-sunspots were unstable and underwent changes in their magnetic fields due to both internal and external forces, and that these changes may have led to the release of stored magnetic energy in the form of coronal material and other emissions.

The Mumford end-injection conjecture is a more robust version of the Asano Mumford conjecture. A different, yet equivalent, formulation posits that any structure with virtual map complexity 1 must have actual map complexity 1. We found a specific class of closed hyperbolic surfaces for which the map complexity is strictly less than the virtual map complexity, assuming Mumford's C-irreducibility conjecture is true. In the context of surface products, we proved that if the virtual map complexity of surfaces S and S' is both 1, then the virtual map complexity of their product is 1.

Computational models of cardiac mechanics, obtained by coupling electrochemical and mechanical phenomena, are effective tools for investigating the structure and function of the heart. However, simulating these models accurately poses significant challenges due to sharply varying length and time scales, making it difficult to employ fine meshes and large time steps. Although the time hierarchy multilevel algorithm (THMAl) has shown promise in addressing these issues, its suitability for parallel computing environments is limited, while the block algebraic multilevel preconditioner (BAMG) suffers from poor performance in adaptive time-stepping applications. In our research, we enhance both preconditioners to make them scalable for parallel computing and robust under adaptive time-stepping schemes. Furthermore, we enhance their preconditioning capabilities by incorporating an eigenvalue solver and a multigrid method. Through comprehensive numerical experiments, we validate the efficiency and performance of these preconditioners on realistic human heart models.

The ever-growing significance of user-generated content is best exemplified by social tagging systems, large-scale platforms that facilitate tag assignment to web resources by users, resulting in a substantial body of data concerning online content usage and user behavior. From a data mining standpoint, user-generated tags present unique opportunities to analyze user behavior and the functional structure of the internet, leading to substantial findings in coherence, collaboration, semantic evolution, and semantic fluctuations. Building on prior studies that uncovered user behavior patterns and the dynamics of user-generated semantics on the web, this research delves further into temporal patterns of reuse, interests sharing, collaborative tagging, and the temporal dynamics and fluctuations of user-generated semantics. Our analysis, based on a comprehensive temporal model of social tagging data, is illustrated using LiveBookmarks.

Recently developed acoustic metagratings offer new possibilities for controlling high-frequency sound waves, and this research examines their performance with O and U band ultrasound. A polymer composite of liquid crystals and resonating spheres is formulated and microfabricated using two-photon lithography, enabling the investigation of acoustic waves at 35 GHz. Simulation and experimental findings demonstrate that microacoustic metagratings can effectively attenuate and polarize high-frequency ultrasound, and the use of 3D printing allows for the production of complex patterns and thus, diverse applications.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of strong solutions for the two-dimensional compressible FENE model, a type of polymer model. Firstly, it establishes the existence of global strong solutions that remain intact over extended periods. Subsequently, it demonstrates that as time progresses, these solutions converge to equilibrium states, with the rate of convergence determined by the distance to the equilibrium and governed by the parameter $\theta$. Additionally, it is shown that in the absence of the parameter $\theta$, the solutions also converge to equilibrium, with the rate of convergence determined by the smallest eigenvalue of the spatial domain and also governed by the parameter $\delta$.

Integrating Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) in cellular networks is a crucial element in mobile backhaul solution. To pave the way for mobile IAB networks, we first need to tackle the uncertainty of wireless backhaul links. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of IAB by discussing key challenges and solutions in paging, data transfer, and wireless link evaluation. The insights gained from these solutions can help in developing viable approaches for addressing IAB challenges.

This study employs two methods, the Sobol' and the Morris sensitivity analysis techniques, to investigate the impact of evolutionary algorithm (EA) hyperparameters on their performance across various benchmark optimization problems. The analysis reveals which parameters and combinations are most relevant and efficient, providing valuable insights for setting these hyperparameters. The results also highlight that setting certain hyperparameters can simplify the process without compromising solution quality, which has the potential to enhance EA design and implementation.

The paper presents compelling reasons behind the wave formula $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$, used extensively in various contexts in physics, in particular on the right-hand side of the wave equation. Although it's often associated with the relativistic relationship $\omega^2=c^2k^2$ and its connection between space and frequency, the paper focuses on nonrelativistic scenarios where $\omega^2\propto k^2$. Despite some mathematically sound justifications for certain expressions, the paper finds most existing arguments inconclusive. It then presents two distinct cases where the wave formula naturally emerges from solutions involving Dirac delta functions. However, it's crucial to note that in both cases, the resulting solutions也只具有周期性, rather than being strictly equal to the original delta functions, implying that this particular wave formula may be viewed more as a limiting case rather than an exact equality.

Despite notable advances in reinforcement learning, numerous challenges remain to be addressed in diverse, complex environments to facilitate broader application. Reinforcement learning research typically concentrates on controlled settings, leaving numerous real-world problems unexplored. Furthermore, existing control theory-focused benchmarks do not fully capture adjustment frequencies or memory constraints that are critical factors in real-world applications. In response, we introduce L2Explorer, a controlled benchmark for continual learning in reinforcement learning settings, which we employ to test algorithms across a variety of tasks. The L2Explorer benchmark is based on a modular framework for environmental modification, allowing for frequent changes. Real-world inspired scenarios, such as product development or network operation, demonstrate that L2Explorer models key frequency and memory constraints present in practical applications, highlighting which algorithms are feasible under such limitations. The L2Explorer benchmark can be accessed at: https://github.com/ai2/L2Explorer.

Liger, a next-generation imaging detector, will be installed at the Department of Terrestrial Microseismology Observatory's Planetarium at Keck Observatory in Hawaii. Liger's advanced imaging capabilities will replace existing cameras by offering superior performance in the Keck Telescope's field of view with exceptional sensitivity and high-speed data acquisition. To handle the enormous data rate Liger will produce, a multi-layered data processing system will be employed to filter and compress data before it's sent to external storage systems. This paper outlines the design of this data processing system and its software interfaces.

In the context of the two-dimensional Euler equation, the initial conditions of a small, periodic, and one-dimensional disturbance result in a flow of waves that asymptotically approach a Couette-like state. The outcome is influenced by the initial amplitude of the disturbance, where a specific type of solution emerges for smaller amplitudes, characterized by a solitary wave and a coupling with the imaginary spectrum, occurring when the disturbance is sufficiently small. Conversely, a different regime is identified for mid-sized amplitudes, resulting in the dissolution of the solitary wave, leaving a residual Couette flow, which is stable but fails to be linearly stable. However, it's important to note that a small perturbation does not destroy the result; instead, the outcome remains unchanged, which is not linked to the initial conditions but rather a characteristic of a specific solution space. Finally, the existence of a small amount of two-dimensional noise in the initial conditions leads to a small, localized turbulence that persists indefinitely.

Our research showcases the optical control of polarized light using a single approach, involving the manipulation of exciton-polariton condensates to modify polarization properties within linearly polarized beams without influencing amplitude or acquiring refractive index changes. This approach relies on two mechanisms: the use of exciton-polariton condensates with parallel and perpendicular dipole moments in relation to the incoming light, and the application of in-plane and out-of-plane dipole interactions respectively. These interactions enable optical control of both polarization angle and birefringence, facilitated by the components of the incoming light field. This fully optical system offers direct optical control of linear polarization features, complementary to other research focusing on optical amplitude and phase adjustments. Furthermore, adding nonlinearity allows for observation of polarization phenomena, such as polarization switching, and observing this effect in a 2D dipole system reveals an observation of Macroscopic Magnetization. This research presents a novel method for manipulating polarization through collective exciton-polariton effects, offering potential for application in polarized light switching and all-optical logic operations for future polarized light processing technologies.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence for the deterministic fractional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation with a nonlocal derivative term, which we develop through the limit of stochastic KPP equations with both a standard and a nonlocal derivative term, resulting in the stochastic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang and fractional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equations, respectively.

In early March 2020, The Bureau for Economic Research, established in collaboration with the South African government, launched an dashboard to collect real-time data concerning COVID-19 in South Africa. This data was sourced through online surveys and web-based reporting channels. The dashboard facilitated research into the pandemic's impact, by providing essential insights into the coronavirus outbreak, South Africa's lockdown measures, and government policy responses. The dashboard's Data Quality Monitoring Team assessed the reliability of the collected data. The research presented in this paper demonstrates how to utilize integrated data and analytical tools to provide data-driven recommendations for high-level decision-making. These recommendations were formulated through analysis by diverse experts, taking into account data quality and limitations. This approach enabled South African officials to make informed decisions regarding policy choices, such as the declaration of a national state of disaster and the implementation of lockdowns.

In 1961, Freiman demonstrated that any subset of the integers with size at least two, specifically denoted as $A$, has a larger subset, represented as $B$, whose cardinality is $3|A|-4$, and every element in $B$ can be expressed as the sum of two elements from $A$. Through an enhanced version of Freiman's result, we demonstrate the existence of $B$ without needing to include any elements expressed as the difference between two elements from $A$.

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved automated detection of diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma using various imaging techniques. This study introduces an innovative approach that combines multiple sources of information from a single, comprehensive eye examination. Specifically, we develop a novel data fusion method that integrates structural and functional information about the eye, and demonstrate its efficacy in diagnosing two major eye conditions. Our proposed method surpasses existing techniques and exhibits potential for real-world clinical implementation.

To tackle limitations in large-scale clinical data for COVID-19, an approach is proposed that utilizes non-invasive chest X-rays. The approach aims to create a dataset for identifying ICU admission potential by incorporating easily accessible patient information such as demographics and clinical history. The underlying concept will be supported by the novel attribute 'pulmonary vascular congestion,' which the researchers demonstrate can be detected in X-rays. The potential benefits of utilizing such accessible attributes for image analysis are discussed. The created dataset, analysis results, and annotation tools are made publicly available.

This study offers a theoretical framework for identifying the boundaries of a sphere within a spherical layered medium using transmission eigenvalues and functions. The proposed method leverages the unique properties of transmission functions, specifically their asymptotic behaviors at distinct boundaries, to determine the transmission eigenvalues and functions. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the transmission functions exhibit node points, allowing for the identification of eigenvalues through the transmission functions themselves. The validity of this approach has been validated through numerical experiments conducted on models representing the Earth and biological tissues, showcasing its capability to not only pinpoint the boundaries but also distinguish between different layers by utilizing node points. The primary advantage of this methodology lies in its reliance on global data, thereby eliminating the need for data collection at high-precision locations, which often poses significant challenges in real-world applications.

To effectively engage with users, understanding their goals is crucial for service-oriented systems.  However, extracting meaningful insights from everyday conversations is challenging, particularly as users' statements are often brief and fragmented.  Drawing from the success of words in short contexts for tasks like classification and representation, the concept of intent in longer conversations has been explored, yet most approaches struggle with the full conversation history due to the difficulty in modeling the entire context.  This paper presents a new solution that overcomes these limitations, involving a two-part approach that begins with pre-training on the complete conversation history and then fine-tunes it on shorter, available segments.  Moreover, a new method called iRep is introduced, which leverages the power of contrastive learning to yield a highly effective intent representation that surpasses previous methods in the realm of intent classification.

The $n$th term of the simplicial group formed by symmetries of Artin generators and relations has a specific notation, denoted as $G_{(n)}$, which corresponds to the $n$th level of a specific simplicial set, particularly one that represents the free simplicial abelian group with its own set of generators, especially given by its $n$th term.

M. K. Szymanski initially proposed an upper limit for the number of subgroups in finite groups, setting it at $2^{n^2+2n}$. This bound was later refined by B. H. Neumann and W. A. Thomas to $2^{n^2+2n-1}$, but it's evident that it cannot be the best possible limit. Our research aims to establish a specific maximum number of subgroups in finite groups of a given order. We have successfully lowered the exponent from $n^2+2n-1$ to $n^2+0.9488n$, and in the context of $p$-solvable groups, to $n^2(1+2/p) + (2/p)^2n$. For prime cyclic groups, we have proven that the number of subgroups does not exceed $n^2(1+2/p)$.

A notable equation, derived from equation (4.1) in reference 2 of Baianu, derived an innovative nonlinear partial differential equation, the h2 equation, which has been referred to as the ABS h2 equation. This equation, although derived from an erroneous premise, seems to possess an intriguing intricate structure, warranting thorough examination and analysis. This motivation has been explored in reference to the need for an exhaustive review of the ABS h2 equation.

One major challenge in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), which involves identifying objects and their relationships in an image, is the problem of false positives. This issue arises due to ambiguous or inherently difficult relationships that are hard to distinguish from one another. A common example includes mistaking a relationship as a person riding an bicycle rather than simply being near it. This work delves into VRD's Vague Relationships category to tackle the problem of ambiguous relationships. After outlining the problems and limitations of current VRD models, we propose an enhanced VRD approach that outperforms existing models in handling Vague Relationships. Our experiment, conducted on the COCO dataset, demonstrates our model's superiority and its potential for improvement on the VRD task, particularly in addressing false positives.

A novel approach has been introduced to analyze the price of quantum correlations in quantum systems undergoing quantum evolution, utilizing weak measurements without requiring full state tomography. This new method determines the maximum price of quantum correlations in bipartite systems, where one subsystem is controlled and used to trigger nonlocal behavior in the other subsystem. Notably, this approach holds true for all initial state configurations and initially local quantum processes. Furthermore, we have analyzed the price of quantum correlations in specific scenarios, including when one qubit becomes entangled with a probe and interacts with a second qubit. These findings demonstrate that, under weak measurements, the price of quantum correlations can be achieved using an optimal range of rotation angles, thereby surpassing the max value obtained through strong measurements and revealing non-trivial nonlocal behavior. This new price of quantum correlations offers a broader definition, encompassing more widely applicable resources of non-trivial quantum behavior.

This paper presents a method for analyzing images containing groups of people, aiming to determine the interactions between them, ultimately generating a graph representing social relationships, i.e. linking connected individuals. A key figure in this process is the social broker, someone capable of facilitating interactions among various groups. Our single, integrated network can identify and annotate person brokering skills within an image, track their progression, and depict these relationships, i.e. connecting people who have interacted with one another through the brokering process. Evaluations using the RGBSD dataset, extracted from news and Wikipedia images, indicate the effectiveness of our approach in visualizing social relationships and significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, achieving a top-performance score of 0.625 at 5 brokering steps. Notably, our method has uncovered subtle insights into brokering skills that were previously overlooked in the dataset, i.e. connecting unrelated individuals over distant geographical areas, i.e. from Italy to the US, as visible in the generated social relationship graphs, i.e. through the use of i.e. ICA for visualization purposes.

Deep neural networks have demonstrated exceptional performance in various visual recognition tasks. Despite the success of deep CNNs, they often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies due to their design. The application of self-attention mechanisms, such as CNNs with CRFs and Transformers, has shown promise in addressing this limitation. However, these approaches can be hindered by a rising computational complexity with input size and lack a clear direction for feature propagation. The use of graph convolutions presents an alternative, offering structured feature extraction, adaptability to input variations, and controlled information flow. Yet, direct application of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) is impractical due to the infinite dimensionality of visual inputs. We develop Dynamic Graph Convolutional Networks (DG-CNNs), a novel architecture that automatically generates and manipulates graphs within CNNS. The DG-CNNs generate graphs based on intermediate feature maps and employ graph-based CNNS to create variants, such as DG-CNN (Full) and DG-CNN (Match). The proposed architecture has achieved impressive results, with the DG-CNN (Match) variant attaining an 81.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-2012 and outperforming existing baselines, including CNNs with CRFs and Transformers. The DG-CNNs are also efficient, with the DG-CNN (Full) variant achieving 78.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-2012 at an inference time of

Optimized hardware is essential for optimized Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) modules, which are efficiently replaced with a single multiplier in software and hardware implementations. Existing algorithms minimize the number of multiplications but neglect the expense of adders, often leading to suboptimal outcomes. To address this shortcoming, a new suboptimal algorithm is proposed that minimizes the sum of the expense of the final sum and intermediate carry-save to two's complement conversion (C2S) circuits in MCM modules. The algorithm seeks to minimize the total expense of adders used in the sum tree, given a fixed expense of the C2S circuit. An alternative approach, exploring the expense of the sum tree as a secondary optimization criterion, is also examined. The primary objective is to minimize the total expense of the MCM module hardware. The algorithm prioritizes minimizing the sum of the expense of the final sum and C2S circuits over the expense of the sum tree.

Quantum machine learning has emerged as a burgeoning field within quantum computing research, driven by the potential for exponential speedups in optimization tasks. Among its key areas is quantum neural network research, which seeks to develop novel quantum algorithms capable of matching the performance of their classical counterparts. This introduction to quantum neural networks covers the historical context of quantum computing methods, an overview of relevant quantum algorithms, optimization challenges, and the application of quantum algorithms to neural network training. It also explores the theoretical underpinnings of quantum neural networks, highlighting their advantages over classical neural networks, before discussing the practical hurdles of quantum technologies.

The radio frequency accelerator community played a crucial role in the historical progression of particle accelerators and will continue to be integral to the future. Despite the long-standing knowledge of their benefits, the technical complexities and diverse nature of RF technologies continue to present challenges in acceleration technologies. These challenges continue to provide opportunities for innovative solutions in various areas including surface technologies, cavities, power systems, and new concepts in RF acceleration. The specialized skills and expertise within the RF community make them invaluable problem-solvers in not only the accelerator community but also across scientific disciplines. This publication, a report from Snowmass 2021, was prepared by the topical group in High Energy Physics: Accelerator Development & Technology (AF7-rf) and encompasses the knowledge and insights of all RF experts contributing to the radiation source community, encompassing both charged particle accelerators and the accelerator-based instrumentation in neutrino and antimatter experiments.

particle physics, capable of unlocking new insights into the Standard Model.
The advantage of using muons, despite their short lifespan, is that they can
effectively probe particle interactions at extremely high energy levels. The
short lifespan of muons also requires the development of advanced muon
accelerators to extend their lifetime and maximize the sensitivity of the
collider. The short-range forces of muons are extremely effective in revealing
patterns of particle behavior at the heart of high-energy interactions. The
muon collider's sensitivity is amplified by the absence of background noise
that typically plagues electron colliders, making the design of a high-sensitivity
experiment both a major opportunity and a significant challenge. The short
