Neural networks for raised text point cloud models improve their geometry through different smoothing methods, but they often produce too-smooth model surfaces that distort the original shape and content. Our research presents a new, effective technique called transformation-unique smoothing to preserve the original point cloud model's features and improve its surface quality. We pre-process the raw data by converting each point into four configuration options and apply four unique smoothing methods, with the network selecting the best configuration and smoothing method. Our model can it also it adaptively choose the most suitable point configuration andsmoothing method. Our approach outperforms the latest related works in terms of surface quality and preserving the original point cloud model's features.

We investigate the creation of distributed networks of Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radars and develop area network access protocols to manage medium access in such systems, aiming to mitigate the impact of range resolution dilution (RMD) caused by mutual interference. Two protocols are proposed: the first is a randomized protocol based on Slotted ALOHA that optimizes the probability of successful transmission, while the is a deterministic variant of Contention Scheduling Control Access (CSCA) that utilizes an optimized decision tree. Both protocols are evaluated through simulations in a standard testing environment.

Examinations of the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect with two-photon absorption effects have shown that photon pairs can be entangled. We've found that the photon photons are not truly entangled; rather, they form a state of entanglement with the exciton due to light-matter interaction. We've discovered that measurements can recover the photon photons in an entangled state, but only if the excitons are destroyed. Two-photon absorption influences the correlation of outgoing photons and can be manipulated to restore it. Additionally, we found that the photon photons are entwined with the excitons, an concept that might offer a framework for categorizing quantum correlations in complex many-body systems.

We develop circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology for compact manifolds like the projective spaces CP(V), leveraging an action on V by complex multiplication, and also establish that the local representation of elliptic co cohomories to polynomials is the local Chern-Weil representation of local K-theory.

Temporal knowledge graph inference is becoming increasingly vital in AI, yet current methods are often hindered by complex models and inefficient representations. These problems are exacerbated by a lack of transparency and difficulty in updating models after initial training. In this research, we tackle a crucial aspect of temporal knowledge graph inference by leveraging a simpler, model-agnostic representation learned through inductive bias and continuous training. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing models on four real-world datasets, consisting of up to one billion triples, even when individual entity and relation embeddings are limited to a smaller size. Furthermore, we discovered that combining continuous representation learning with a traditional transition model yields superior results compared to deep learning-based baseline models. Notably, our approach offers the advantage of easily integrating new knowledge into the temporal knowledge graph without needing to retrain the model.

In a specific type of ground state with one gluon, the non-perturbative influence on the gluon condense effect is being investigated using the Landau gauge, resulting in an anharmonic, frequency-dependent frequency shift that aligns with calculations from the David model, along with a low-frequency imaginary component, indicating damping. Furthermore, the DRE model, particularly its landau gauge, exhibits a positive, frequency-dependent frequency-dependent mass squared, which varies from a negative value in the absence of the gluon, indicating a phase transition, however, this feature disappears in the deconfining, high-temperature QGP due to the Landau gauge, leading to a positive, negative, and zero mass squared in the lattice, the maximal Abelian gauge, and the Azepe gauge, respectively.

We have developed a demonstration of Bell nonlocality that does not rely on specific conditions, using perfect correlations in a scenario with multiple outcomes and non-local realism with local determinism, in contrast to stochastic local deterministic models, which can simulate statistical local deterministic models. Our model does not require specific correlations to be achievable due to local hidden variable theories, allowing it to be applied in real experiments to rigorously demonstrate Bell nonlocality without inequalities.

In search of novel solutions to the longstanding problems of localizing and detecting objects, this paper presents a method to generate image templates via horizontal lines, then matches them with image content. Our approach, distinct from existing methods, uses local features to identify the optimal position of these lines. We propose placing multiple horizontal lines within a search region to increase the accuracy of matching. To minimize computational costs, we have implemented an efficient line matcher with reduced complexity. Furthermore, our method excels in tracking moving lines, proving effective for lines with varying orientations. As a result, our method achieves a satisfactory compromise between speed and performance. Experimental findings demonstrate that our method localizes linear features with a 0.3-pixel average accuracy. We provide a open-source implementation, available at https://github.com/alexeykuzin/flatlines.

A thorough examination was carried out to investigate the impacts of hydrogen impurities on the superconducting capabilities of sulfur hydride for temperatures above zero kelvin. Our comprehensive studies employed sophisticated methodologies to investigate the purity, structural, thermodynamic, and electronic characteristics of sulfur hydride in its $\epsilon$-phase. The superconducting properties of sulfur hydride were then evaluated using two distinct methods: the Eilenberger method and the Matsubara superconductor theory. The results revealed that sulfur hydride exhibits very weak superconductivity at temperatures near 270 kelvin with minimal hydrogen substitution, significantly falling below its previously predicted critical temperature of 90 kelvin. The influence of potassium impurities increased sulfur hydride's critical temperature to approximately 27 kelvin. The findings indicate that sulfur hydride's superconducting behavior originates from the presence of hydrogen as an intrinsic component, rather than being the primary driver of this phenomenon.

Cloud infrastructure depends heavily on efficient CPU allocation strategies to ensure optimal resource management and application performance. The traditional allocation methods often involve rounding, leading to suboptimal outcomes and increased waste. The Flattened Partitioning approach combines rounding with the Hyperthreading technique to propose an innovative method for CPU allocation in cloud environments. The Fractal partitioning method divides CPUs into sections based on performance characteristics, facilitating faster and more accurate allocation. The Fractal approach outperforms existing solutions by improving CPU allocation efficiency by up to 20% and enhancing applications' CPU usage and profitability. The Fractal method enables service providers to negotiate better terms and conditions with customers based on actual CPU usage and returns. The Fractal approach represents a significant advancement in CPU allocation and resource management for cloud-based APAs, offering improved profit and more accurate CPU usage and pricing negotiations.

We demonstrate that characteristic zeros for the special orthogonal group SO(0) are identical to those of the upper triangular special orthogonal group, differing from the characteristics of the unitary group, due to the presence of charm. This equivalence also extends to the Lorentz group, SO(1,0). The equivalence values increase with the addition of supple components, and groups, including SU(N) and Spin(0), exhibit high stiffness. This study emphasizes the flexibility and rigidity properties exhibited by these groups under expansion.

Highway driving systems that can operate independently in case of failure are designed to maintain safety during transitions between various stages of automation. This research presents an extensive examination of these transition phases, focusing on how the system gracefully fails when full control is relinquished to the driver. We employ fail-safe techniques, such as imposing time limits on automated systems and immediately alerting the driver with non-negotiable warnings, to ensure a smooth handover of control. We develop an design for this examination using formal methods in formal specification and validation, incorporating both continuous and discrete elements. Additionally, we explore the concept of valid state interval to guarantee that the driving system's safety measures are never compromised.

This research explores a method of clustering dynamical systems based on the anticipated impact of the generated time series. The proposed approach initially identifies potential extreme events in the phase space of each system using the maximum of a specific metric. Subsequent analysis of these events reveals systems with similar structures and dynamics, even in the absence of clear attractors. The proposed method's application is demonstrated on three well-known nonlinear systems, and its potential is further illustrated through the exploration of an experimentally-relevant dataset of weakly coupled chaotic systems.

This note compares three infinite matrix Leibnizian calculus approaches, aiming to illustrate their benefits and describe their fundamental principles. The techniques are non-standard analysis, axiomatic regularized non-standard analysis, and triple-O-regularization. The study explores how to treat infinitesimals and infinity within an axiomatic framework, emphasizing their historical context and mathematical applications.

Recent advancements in technology have made HI intensity mapping a highly promising approach for conducting large-scale scientific research into the universe. As a result, experiments utilizing the MFU instrument at VLA and KATRRE at SKA will generate terabytes of data, posing significant challenges for foreground removal and analysis. To address this challenge, we have developed a framework, known as disturbance theory, which can guide the HI intensity mapping power spectrum analysis. Furthermore, we have integrated this framework with simulation tools, such as SILICON and PySM, to accurately model the HI emission. However, the specific impact of foreground removal on the HI emission is beyond the scope of disturbance theory, requiring additional, more complex models. To bridge this gap, we have developed a new converter, which can translate the HI emission models into the HI emission power spectrum, which then incorporates cosmological signals along with other interference, such as solar system foregrounds. This approach, centered around the concept of foreground removal effects, offers a versatile pathway for analyzing the HI emission power spectrum, which can be applied regardless of the specific method used for foreground removal.

Our analysis has specific objectives. Firstly, we're exploring the relationship between independent sets and their ability to interact with linear combinations of basis vectors, similar to the conjecture by Brouwer and Huysmans. We're particularly interested in the maximum possible size of independent sets, as well as the sets comprising the support of linear combinations of basis vectors. Another aim is to determine the relationships, or lack thereof, between independent sets and these sets, as well as the relationship between a set and it's scaled versions.

Recommender systems are designed to analyze user preferences in order to provide personalized suggestions for items that users may be interested in. There is an ongoing need to refine these systems to increase their effectiveness and adaptability. In this paper, a research question is explored to assess the potential of combining multiple recommender system methods to improve overall performance. Numerous recommender system approaches have been developed, each with its own set of advantages and limitations. Two main types of methods are widely used: collaborative filtering and content-based systems. Context-aware content-based methods consider the specific situation at hand, while behavior-based methods draw on user interactions with items and their neighbors. To enhance context-based methods, this paper proposes integrating behavior-based techniques. The proposed hybrid method draws on both supervised learning principles, used in behavior-based methods, and unsupervised learning principles, used in context-based methods. The suggestion is that this integration can lead to improved performance, particularly when dealing with sparse data, a common issue in recommender systems. The effectiveness of the proposed method is tested using the Python sparse matrix library. The approach being explored has the potential to be applied in various fields, such as biomedicine, finance, and e-commerce, making it a viable candidate for broader implementation.

Consider an arbitrary complex symmetric matrix with independent random entries, and let polynomials of its entries define a type B open set if the resulting algebraic variety consists of irreducible connected components. Building upon earlier findings for random matrices of various types, particularly those with real or complex entries, we prove that certain matrix combinations are type B open with high probability, given certain conditions, thus demonstrating almost sure freeness of their associated types. Additionally, we establish the free relationship between two matrices, one of which has real, symmetric, or complex symmetric distribution, under the condition of full rank.

We examine the problem of detecting timing constraints in transition systems at a specific state, along with its universal and existential variants. The original problem formulation is adapted for software testing purposes, focusing on identifying timed properties within software systems. The problem has been addressed for general transition systems, and we've revisited this solution in the context of software testing.

The production process of $a_0(980)-f_0(2987)$ in $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi N$ interactions is examined. Utilizing complex vector robustness (CVB) analysis, calculations indicate that this production process is feasible and the $S$-wave contribution significantly outweighs the $P$-wave contribution. Conversely, in the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0$ transition, the $P$-wave contribution dominates over the $S$wave contribution, with the latter possibly indicating the presence of dynamical effects. In the decay of $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \eta$, the $S$-wave and $P$-wave contributions are roughly comparable, with considerations of the final state interaction between these mesons necessary, particularly in the context of their blending around the 1 GeV threshold, with the $S$-wave more strongly influenced than the $P$-wave. Finally, based on lattice QCD data and phenomenological models, the mass values of the $S$-wave and $P$-wave in the decay of $a_0(980)-f_0(2987)$ are estimated to be approximately 1030 MeV and 1060 MeV, respectively, with the latter supported by recent data on the $a_2(12

The GRAVITY observing mode utilizes four single-mode fibers as inputs to a unique combination of beam splitters, providing both the spatial separation and spectral resolution necessary for astrometric and spectrographic analysis. Our investigations into the observing mode's chromatic behavior have produced significant results. We presented an overview of the gravity observing mode and characterized its performance in astrometry and spectrography. We also discussed the accuracy of the centroiding method used for target astrometric assessment, as well as the resolution achievable through cross-correlation for spectral analysis.

The application of approximation algorithms to geometric problems has seen significant advancement, with many approaches leveraging the property of doubling spaces, where efficient schemes exist. However, these benefits aren't guaranteed for all problems until disproven through counterexamples. In this paper, a counterexample to $k$-center clustering is provided, showing a constant-factor approximation with freedom dimension one, whereas this implies unbounded approximation ratios when combining with doubling dimension.

In this study, the uniqueness of entire functions that have their finite order and contain their shifted versions within the same space was investigated, incorporating critical conditions related to the counting measure of zeros when the order is less than three halves.

This research explores the feasibility of solving polynomial linear systems by leveraging random sampling and incurring some inaccuracies, while maintaining efficiencyExceeding a predetermined number of iterations is unnecessary; earlier exit points accelerate the process, specifically, the FGM method can solve an n-dimensional system with m monomials and r errors using only O((r+r^2)m + ((r+r^2)lm + r^2m^2)) operations. This optimum efficiency matches established standards for mistake-precise methods and surpasses existing limits for systems with errors, while employing a technique accelerating exit points to minimize computational requirements.

The dynamic behavior of an open quantum system, whose parity is protected, was investigated in the context of a specific two-level setup. Due to the system's symmetry, it displays an emission pattern that is uniformly distributed, regardless of the initial state configuration. However, when the system is coupled with environmental interaction, its emission intensity variations appear, resulting in off-resonant light emission. Notably, the influence of the system's symmetry remains prevalent when adjusting the environmental interaction.

A simple yet accurate theoretical model is developed to describe the thermodynamic properties of an equilibrium plasma composed of atoms, ions, and electrons, particularly those involving non-hydrogen alkali elements. The proposed model builds upon the law of mass conservation to create a precise equation of state, offering an alternative to complex numerical computations or more intricate analytical methods. The model is validated by comparing its predictions with those from a widely-used thermodynamic database, demonstrating excellent agreement. Notably, the model is 100 to 1,000 times faster in calculating temperature and density of the ideal gas mixture, and is found to be applicable within a specific temperature range, with an associated margin of error of 0.01 to 0.1%.

The behavior of vector mesons in a chiral asymmetric vacuum state of fermions is studied, focusing on the impact of chiral asymmetry induced by fermionic vacuum charges, particularly on the $J/\Psi$ state, within the framework of a three-point function analysis involving one photon and two light pions. This research investigates whether chiral symmetry breaking in the fermionic vacuum causes observable changes in the masses of heavy vector mesons, revealing that such symmetry breaking leads to modifications in meson spectrum parameters, though the magnitude of these modifications is negligible for $J/\Psi$ due to its large mass relative to the involved quarks' masses. This phenomenon is understood through the principles of hidden flavor symmetry and the dominance of color Coulomb forces in binding quark-antiquark pairs, which suppresses the symmetry breaking effect despite the meson being sensitive to the vacuum charge.

This research investigates the estimation of network size in a small-world environment, where nodes are interconnected through local and long-range links. Each node employs a randomized counter that is updated based on the number of messages received from both neighboring nodes and those that traverse the network, known as over-the-top messages. It is proven that the estimated size converges at a linear rate when receiving only over-the-top messages in a fully connected network with unreliable sources. Furthermore, the study is expanded to a more complex scenario with imperfect sources, where it is shown that the estimate can converge under specific topological constraints. To address the challenge of nodes being controlled by unreliable sources, we developed an estimation algorithm supported by a verification algorithm, known as the Byzantine filter. This filter integrates the behavior of nodes and their incoming messages to filter out unreliable sources and generate an estimate of the network size. It is proven that the filter can accurately distinguish valid over-the-top messages from those controlled by unreliable sources with high probability. Finally, we evaluated the proposed algorithm on both grid and small-world networks, demonstrating its effectiveness in estimating the network size.

In numerical relativity, the initial data constraints (CDC) pose a significant challenge due to their complex, coupled, and non-linear nature. Our proposed method, CTTK, addresses this challenge by transforming the standard CDC into a different format and solving the resulting system using PDE-based approaches to obtain the spatial metric, while simultaneously solving for the trace-free part of the extrinsic curvature.

The JUNO experiment, being the largest water-Cherenkov detector project, employs 32,000 tons of water and 50 kilotons of liquid scintillator alongside 20-inch photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to detect neutrinos. For its sensitivity and energy resolution requirements, the PMTs used in JUNO need to have consistent mass and material properties. To verify these characteristics, a testing procedure was conducted at the Shaoxing detector fabrication site using newly acquired 20-inch PMTs. Specifically, the linear relationship between voltage and photoelectron count was verified using electron yields and nitrogen gas. Moreover, metal plating and mass screening methods were performed on these PMTs. The results of the mass screening and electrical tests revealed that 656 out of 800 tested PMTs met JUNO's performance standards. The data obtained from the testing process contributed significantly to understanding the mass screening, mass production, and mass installation processes of the PMTs used in JUNO.

Predicting how time series data changes is crucial in many fields, but traditional approaches like multilayer perceptrons and long short-term memory networks are inflexible in capturing complex patterns. The limitations of these models are addressed by incorporating a multilayer graph into the prediction models, using the graph's structure to represent data features and its properties to capture dynamic relationships. Recent efforts have focused on learning graph features and properties from data, but few have developed fully adaptive models that optimize both simultaneously. This paper introduces a novel, end-to-end learning approach called ADAGCN, which uses neural networks to define graphs and their properties, and demonstrates its superiority to existing methods on synthetic and real-world prediction tasks.

Astronomical observations in non-long-axis-aligned modes are affected by atmospheric dispersion, which varies with wavelength and requires mitigation using specialized hardware. This necessary equipment, paired with the varied optical setups of modern telescopes, has rendered on-sky AD measurements highly diverse. This project endeavors to establish a consistent framework for describing atmospheric dispersion models, facilitating the comparison of different on-sky measurements within a unified mathematical framework. Our proposed description models the Earth's atmosphere as a series of isothermal layers and the dispersion as a combination of refractive indices and physical thicknesses, with various teams reporting their own on-sky measurements in the form of index of refraction profiles, refractive dispersion, and the Abbe number. This paper proposes a description model for the atmospheric dispersion and Fitting B-splines to Cauchy's model of the atmospheric dispersion, with the proposed framework already in use by multiple on-sky measurement teams.

In the realm of semi-supervised learning, Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) functions as a multi-instructor labeled distillation approach, leveraging multiple reliable models to enhance the representation of unlabeled data and improving overall performance. Unlike traditional distillation methods that require extensive annotation of selected unlabeled data, PILE generates pair-wise constraints from reliable models for every semi-supervised sample, eliminating the need for such annotation and reducing the number of distillation instructors to one, without sacrificing performance. Furthermore, our comprehensive analysis uncovers the impact of varying instructor labels on PILE's overall effectiveness.

We've created a new method to look for shadow matter using ultra-light bosons as evidence, and we've devised an experiment to verify its viability. Our approach simulates the impact of shadow matter on X-ray photons, and we've explored the potential of correlation techniques to amplify this signal. A historical dataset from the Chandra X-ray Observatory was analyzed to estimate a correlation and compare its validity to theoretical predictions. Our findings suggest that further research into this topic and refinement of the proposed experiment may lead to a significant advancement in detecting shadow matter.

This paper explores the concept of uniqueness for Bregenzin's basis pursuit problem, which models the reconstruction of a one-dimensional function from its noisy measurements of integrals against given functions. The paper's main contribution is establishing the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this problem, with an emphasis on how these conditions depend on given functions and noise levels. Additionally, the paper identifies specific scenarios under which a solution is guaranteed to be unique.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. This framework separates a compiler front-end from a compiler backend, with the latter responsible for translating P4 programs into the switch-specific binary format known as NetOp. Our work focuses on an open-source P4 backend for V1Model with the P4Utils compiler front-end, emphasizing efficient compiler optimizations and innovative techniques for reducing the overall size of P4 programs while maintaining their original functionality. This study compares our compiler with four other backends from the literature and presents a novel approach for shrinking P4 programs prior to compilation to reduce the final program size. Our results reveal that both of our optimizations yield a 19.6% decrease in the total size of P4 programs, which has significant implications for deploying large P4 programs on resource-constrained hardware.

In numerical magnetohydrodynamics, the continuous interpolation method employing a mesh-independent function space and a space-advancing approach via the solution of a linear system ensures stability and stability of the MHD system's discretisation. Nevertheless, the choice of finite element can significantly influence the accuracy of the resulting numerical solutions by either preserving or deforming the magnetic field. This work examines the performance of the Raviart-Thomas element on the most basic quadrilateral mesh. We discover that the local averaging approach used to interpolate the magnetic field in the vector transport equation introduces errors specific to the mesh topology, which the present study seeks to correct. Various modifications are proposed and evaluated, ultimately identifying an effective method. We then validate the improved element's efficacy through numerical tests.

Federated learning's distributed model training method makes it an ideal solution for addressing fairness and privacy concerns in distributed machine learning.  Drawing on the connections between fairness, privacy, and hyperparameter optimization, this paper investigates the role of federated learning in harmonicizing fairness and privacy.  Specifically, the research examines the effects of federated averaging, a crucial technique for ensuring both fairness and privacy, on model performance.  During training, this procedure is applied to the weights of machine learning models, with implications for fairness and privacy.  In our study, we utilize benchmark datasets and experiments to analyze the impact of federated averaging on the models' fairness and privacy performance.  Additionally, we explore how federated learning encodes client information, which influences both fairness and privacy outcomes.  In addressing these issues, we introduce a novel approach using meta-learning, treating the federated averaging process as a client-specific characteristic.  The results of our investigations and the meta-learning-based method offer new insights and solutions for enhancing the fairness and privacy performance of federated learning models.

Using (pb)(pb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7.3 TeV, 
the LHCb experiment gathered an equivalent data sample of 3.03 fb$^{-1}$. 
This data was analyzed to search for the $B_c^+(1D)$ bottom-charm meson, 
which involves detecting it via its decay into a $J/\psi$ and a $\pi^+$ particle. 
Our analysis, based on detecting the $B_c^+(1D)$ signal through the difference 
between observed and expected yields that can be attributed to background noise, 
reveals the $B_c^+(1D)$ at a 4.2 standard deviation level of significance without 
accounting for statistical testing outcomes. 
The $B_c^+(1D)$ is observed with the following characteristics: a p$_T$ greater 
than 2.5 GeV/c, and $p_{\mathrm{T}}^{J/\psi}$ within 8.5 to 20.5 GeV/c, 
together with an invariant mass greater than 6.45 GeV, but less than 6.85 GeV. 
When integrating over these $B_c^+$ parameters, the $B_c^+(1D)$ production is 
determined to have a relative branching ratio, which is 6.4$^{+2.3}_{-2.0}$ 
times

A new class of estimators, known as continuous-stage Runge-Kutta estimators, is introduced in this study to approximate the solution trajectory of a differential equation. The accuracy of this estimator is analyzed in terms of its convergence rate and an optimal estimator is identified within this class, achieving a specific order of accuracy. The optimality of this estimator is also established in the context of a related random process, known as Euler-Maruyama, for a stochastic differential equation.

This paper introduces a regulatory mechanism called Regional Critic Training (RCT) to improve the performance of deep neural networks in large-scale model parallel learning setups. The RCT framework addresses a critical issue of local parameter optimization by incorporating spatial awareness into the training process. Specifically, RCT employs distinct checkpoints for model layers across tensor parallel groups and trains a neural network-based critic to evaluate the performance of each checkpoint's local group. This is achieved by minimizing spatial prediction errors, thereby enhancing the spatial awareness of the critic. Experimental results on the ALBERT model have demonstrated the significant impact of spatial awareness on the convergence speed and overall convergence quality in deep learning models. Additionally, RCT can be easily integrated into existing training pipelines with minimal overhead in terms of memory and communication costs.

In a three-dimensional Argand attractor system with dissipation reduced below a certain threshold, the largest basinal attractor unexpectedly grows, after initially shrinking at strong dissipation. This sudden expansion, which was not seen in similar systems with reduced complexity, occurs when the system's topological structure changes from fully connected to fragmented. As the weak dissipation increases, the basinal attractor fluctuates wildly and only settles after significantly outweighing the other attractors, at which point it exhibits enhanced phase mixing and intricate folding. This intricate internal organization, combined with its rapid initial development, creates a highly effective trapping area for the basinal attractor, making its surface the most intricate of all attractors in the parameter space and producing primary chaos strips. These features are uniquely associated with the basinal attractor and are not seen in the other two coexisting attractors.

We investigate hypothetical long-lived particles that are produced when particles of zero mass gain flavor and consider their potential as new sources of extremely rare, long-lived, doubly flavor-changing (DFC) particles. These particles, which have been largely overlooked in previous research, are predicted to gain long lifetimes due to effects arising from non-degeneracies in the masses of these hypothetical particles. We primarily examine scenarios where these long-lived particles are photons, neutrons, or pseudoscalar particles with zero spin, interacting via loop processes. We also discuss the potential for greater longevity in scenarios where flavor is changed at tree level. We analyze various constraints on these long-lived particles from both direct searches and indirect flavor searches, focusing particularly on constraints that are not as stringent as before. We explore regions of parameters that are not as restricted, which can result in DFC lifetimes that are deflected.

This study introduces the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) designed for recognizing human activities within unsegmented videos. Focusing on attention mechanisms, HAN is explicitly constructed to identify and prioritize regions vital for understanding activities, thereby diminishing the influence of distracting background elements. Building upon the Extended Optical Flow (EOF) framework, which effectively captures the spatio-temporal flow patterns of objects within videos, HAN integrates the sequential structure and contextual connections of video frames to further enhance its performance. Further optimization comes from integrating a contrastive loss and background attention module into the EOF framework. When evaluated on two public datasets, HAN achieved state-of-the-art results on UCF101-24-40 and matched the leading performance on UCFSuites.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties and censorship of a charged, negative space curvature black hole in an asymptotic space with no horizon. We explored how the temperature and entropy evolve under the influence of an external scalar field and found that their interactions significantly impact the black hole's thermodynamic characteristics. Our analysis using the Rao equation revealed the presence of two singularities, revealing that only certain ranges of the inner and outer horizon radii result in a non-zero temperature. Consequently, when considering small disturbances, we assessed the thermodynamic behavior of the system, discovering that its core lies in the difference between the perturbations of the temperature and entropy. Our research demonstrated that this temperature-sentropy interaction adheres to the feeble version of the cosmic censorship hypothesis, revealing interesting and significant relationships in the system.

The phenomenon of starlight becoming visible happens when a star's illumination makes it easier to see objects that were previously obscured by night. This phenomenon is relevant to businesses, as people tend to engage in more recreational and leisure activities at night than during the day. The psychological impact of night-time darkness also comes into play. This phenomenon is analogous to the awakening of consciousness, as understood by psychologists. Psychology emphasizes the importance of balance and harmony, with a particular focus on the relationship between work and play. Play, in particular, has a stimulating effect, prompting individuals to take risks and explore their surroundings in a controlled manner. On a cosmic scale, this phenomenon can be related to the development of intelligent life and the emergence of starlight across the universe. Given the vast number of stars in the universe, at least one of them is likely to have planetary systems capable of supporting life and, eventually, intelligent life that creates its own light.

Using the Nested Sampling method, we have derived formulas for various entropy concepts for both continuous and discrete systems. These formulas rely on partitioning the prior parameter space into a set of nested points. The results show that these entropies are generally dependent on the specific NS algorithm used, making them entropy measures in the broad sense. To achieve algorithm-independent entropy measures, we have also developed alternative formulas. The relative entropy and free energy of a model can be determined by evaluating the entropy of its posterior and comparing it to the entropy of the prior. The proposed methods enable the relative entropy and free energy to be calculated directly from the samples generated during NS, thus eliminating the need for additional sampling for tempering or variational inference. Furthermore, our approach allows the free energy of a model to be calculated directly from the results of NS. The findings also extend to a space representing the model itself, where we can calculate the entropy rate of a discrete stochastic process. The derivation of these formulas relies heavily on understanding how the specific NS algorithm treats volume within its parameter space.

We explore a time-dependent measure μ_t defined on R x [0,∞) that projects to a finite measure m on R, which we use to solve the problem:
  ∂u/∂t + ∂f(u)/∂x = 0 in μ_t, with support in R+, and u, which maps R+ into R, being measurable. Here, u acts as a random variable with distribution μ_t.
We're investigating whether this model aligns with the principle of mass conservation in the face of uncertainty represented by μ_t.
It turns out that a measure μ_t that projects to m and satisfies the above equation must first and always project to the same measure m, which represents the conserved quantity u.
This discovery highlights the importance of maintaining both determinism and randomness as fundamental principles.

The proliferation of IoT devices has accelerated innovation and advancement, yet concomitantly exposed significant vulnerabilities in the security of IoT systems. The diversity of IoT devices and protocols employed poses a challenge for intrusion detection systems, which are tasked with identifying malicious activity across a array of devices utilizing varying communication methods. In this research, we develop NBcoded, a lightweight machine learning-based detector capable of distinguishing between 12 distinct types of intrusions present on IoT devices, including 5-based, 6-based, and 7-based attacks. We compare NBcoded to existing, leading detection systems, and demonstrate its efficiency, particularly in comparison to Autoencoder, a deep learning-based method, showing NBcoded to be a more resource-efficient solution.

We calculate precise growth rates for solvable groups, starting with the basics of what a growth rate is and the concepts of a growth ball and a growth function, before moving on to the more complex topic of growth spheres and its growth function.

Epidemiologists seek effective bioterror response strategies, necessitating detection of abnormal biological movement patterns within populations. To this end, novel algorithms have been developed to identify and track movement within surveillance footage, analyzing the behavior of insects, animals, and humans, leveraging the properties of fluid dynamics. This research presents a comprehensive evaluation of these algorithms, along with the most advanced methods for detecting biological activity, presenting the results of empirical testing on diverse datasets. Furthermore, the study proposes innovative techniques for detecting large gatherings of humans, by adapting and refining existing computer vision methods, and presents the results of practical applications in the e-bioterror detection system.

Optimizing power grid operations is a critical economic issue. We apply the power flow network concept to solve a constrained optimization problem. The network's constraints are reformulated in the form of $N$ Ising spins. Using the quantum annealing technique, we aim to find the minimum-energy state that satisfies these constraints. Our approach was tested on real-world power grid instances, including the Western Interconnect, New York, and Texas grids, within the OpenQASM framework.

In search for a comprehensive physical theory, machine learning models are being employed to analyze complex systems like the Double Copy of Super Yang-Mills theory, leveraging data-driven approaches to simulate intricate mathematical structures such as color-kinematics duality and gravity/elastivity numerics, along with identifying the KLT formula, simultaneously detecting discrepancies such as the positivity bounds in the aforementioned system, ultimately leading to a new algorithm for extracting differential equations from scattering data, demonstrated by its success in reconstructing the QED Born differential equations.

This analysis searches for heavy, charged particles that live for a long time and produce very little visible decay product following interaction with normal matter. The study utilized the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and collected data between 2015 and 2018. The observed data were compared to a Standard Model simulation, without finding any significant differences. Based on these observations, limits were set on the frequency of the particles being searched for, with results also including predictions derived from two distinct particle physics models. Specifically, the study determined cross-section significance levels within the mass range of 60 to 1200 GeV for ions that travel more than 1 meter and produce a visible decay product for a particle that interacts with a proton by leaving a track in a detector with a specific d0 value greater than 0.3 mm. Additionally, the study set significance levels within a mass range of 2000 to 200 GeV for ions that travel more than 2 meters and produce a visible decay product for a particle that interacts with a proton by leaving a track in a detector with a d0 value greater than 1 mm. These findings include results from the standard model of particle physics and the type of interactions between a proton and a neutron. The study also presented significance levels for two theoretical models of heavier particles and their visible decay into a particle that interacts with a proton by leaving a track in a detector with a specific

The demand for high performance integrated single-photon sources using III-V material quantum dots is increasing. These sources, particularly those integrating ridge waveguides and embedded quantum dots, offer superior efficiency and are compatible with advanced integration techniques. However, integrating the resonance properties of the ridge waveguide into the quantum dot's emission can reduce the overall efficiency. This paper presents detailed analysis on maximizing the efficiency of the desired polarization in this type of single-photon source, incorporating recent advancements. Our research indicates that a QCWH structure with type-II confinement outperforms the traditional SEH structure. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential for achieving near-unity polarization efficiency and quantum efficiency. Our findings suggest that integrated III-V SSPC sources based on QCWH are more efficient than SEH sources, and both can be effectively integrated with waveguide-based micro-resonators to enhance their applicability in quantum communication applications.

This study offers an in-depth examination of the boson peak in non-crystalline substances through the lens of neutron scattering. It begins with a comprehensive explanation of the concept's origins and experimental verification, subsequently investigating how the boson peak is portrayed by various neutron scattering methods, namely elastic light scattering (ELS), neutron specific heat, and intermediate scattering functions. It further examines how the nature of the glass relaxes over time using time-resolved techniques. A pivotal aspect of this review involves elucidating the distinctions between the dynamic characteristics of the boson peak entities identified via various techniques, ultimately showcasing how these findings contribute to the nuanced comprehension of the glass's exceptional properties.

High-precision predictions from the Standard Model are crucial for finding evidence of new physics at major projects like the LHC. When calculating multi-loop contributions in perturbation theory, complex expressions with numerous integrals need to be evaluated, and progress in this area is driven by advances in computation techniques for rational functions. This document summarizes a method for handling two-loop scalar Feynman integrals that are frequently encountered at the LHC, involving multiple powers of mass and scalars such as polylogarithms and elliptic curves.

In scattering systems, there's a connection between how energy flows through and the processes of forward and backward reflection, which under specific conditions results in a universal relationship that may help improve the accuracy of measurements in complex environments and analyze the behavior of scattered light in diverse systems. This principle can also be applied in other areas, such as using forward reflection data to calculate backward reflection data in cases where direct measurement isn't feasible, using energy deposition-related metrics to develop new methods for obtaining transmission data in systems with irregular shapes, and using the same metrics in systems where there's no direct path for energy to travel, such as in problems of complete scattering.

Multi-objective optimization seeks to discover all possible solutions that optimally balance multiple objectives. In contrast, phenotypic diversity optimization aims to find the full range of solutions that result from multiple perspectives on a single objective. The concept of phenotypic diversity was initially introduced to study organism variations and was later applied to data analysis. In the field of optimization, it was used to develop a new optimization technique that creates diverse solutions. This paper explores the nature of phenotypic diversity, presenting it as an extension of the Pareto set. The diversity of solutions' characteristics is quantified, and different methods for measuring phenotypic diversity are evaluated for their practical use in creating diverse solution sets. The research also demonstrates how to incorporate the phenotypic diversity into an optimization process without relying on genetic algorithms.

A three-dimensional stable roommates problem was solved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding two-object stable roommates solutions. The algorithm leverages the properties of additive separate preferences to optimize the computational process, which previously took n to the power of five as its most complex operation. By improving the computational complexity to partiate numbers, we were able to solve this problem more efficiently. Our implementation integrates seamlessly with MIPLIBv10's MiQP benchmark, which offers a free set of instances for testing purposes.

This letter examines how different mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, and we model their contributions within a valley Hamiltonian. It's discovered that two mechanisms, forward scattering due to long-range Coulomb interaction coupled with phonons and intervalley scattering via the deformation potential, do not affect valley polarization. However, it's demonstrated that two other mechanisms, scattering mediated by the dipole interaction between electrons and the dipolar deformation of the lattice, and the relaxation rate limitation imposed by the sum rule condition, can influence valley physics in two-dimensional layers. The impact of these mechanisms is visibly seen in scenarios such as spin-orbital scattering in the presence of gate charges and valley polarization constrained within a sum rule framework.

A cloud is an ideal compact subset in the Gromov-Hausdorff category. We define a cloud center as having radii that reach its extremal distance from any point outside the cloud. We establish that every cloud with a specified diameter lower bound possesses a unique center. We define a subclass called n-clouds with bounded local curvature and prove the completeness of this subclass as well as its closure under certain operations. We establish that the dimension of this subclass is equal to the value of 7.

This paper presents a print patch antenna designed for mm-wave applications, optimized to be effective across broad bandwidth and diverse angles of reception. Operating within the 42-88 GHz range, this mm-wave antenna achieves a significant frequency ratio of 2.07:1. It features a broadside design, utilizing the ground plane as the radiating element, achieving substantial broadside performance without needing complex feed structures. As a result, this mm-wave antenna boasts substantial gain and consistent input impedance across its full bandwidth. Moreover, the design's simplicity makes it highly suitable for applications in Software Defined Radios (SDR) and other technologies requiring cost-effective and space-efficient antenna designs.

Researchers believe that fault-tolerant quantum computation will play a vital role in advancing technology, yet creating such systems remains challenging. Recent advancements in machine learning, particularly in reinforcement learning, have led to a breakthrough, enabling a novel method that allows this work to be accomplished via reinforcement learning. Our investigation centers on this method, which we term reinforcement learning coding, as it enables creation of error correcting circuits through systematic exploration. This approach can generate a circuit that's either more fault tolerant or uses fewer physical qubits, thus outperforming traditional methods. Furthermore, our research reveals that this method also has the capability to learn new noise models or improve existing ones, potentially leading to improvements in their accuracy.

Advanced metrology in the sub-Heisenberg limit can be accomplished with nonclassical states, such as those produced by the interaction of a cavity QED system involving two level-jump processes. Assuming the availability of sensors with the capacity to detect these interactions, enhanced limit for phase estimation is predicted. We investigate the maximum achievable improvement in phase estimation precision within a network of two cavities and a license key, given that measurements can be performed only at the output of one of the two sensors. We find that if the two sensors interact symmetrically, pulling from the same direction, the maximum not-Heisenberg limit is predicted, and this maximum is achieved when the reflection coefficients of the sensors approach 1. We also explore the relationship between metrological performance and the nonclassical properties of the state produced by the interaction, such as the fidelity with single photon states, and find that these performances correlate positively. We also investigate whether entanglement between the cavity mode and the atomic state of the emitter can be detected through measurements of output atomic photons, and find that these performances are limited by the coupling of the cavity and atomic level-structures. We also explore the maximum achievable improvement in phase estimation precision within a two-cavity network, given that measurements can be performed only at the output of one of the two sensors. The PHENIX Collaboration measured the correlations of direct photons and hadrons in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV. By comparing these measurements, we can quantify the impact of interactions between the emitted particles and the hot nuclear matter. Our analysis shows that in Au$+$Au collisions, the photon-hadron correlation function is suppressed relative to $d$$+$Au collisions, and this suppression is dependent on the number of participating nucleons and the transverse momentum of the emitted particles. Additionally, we observe that as the hadron's transverse momentum increases, the suppression decreases, which could be attributed to reduced medium interactions.

Quantum simulations of complex fermionic systems pose significant challenges, specifically in mapping their non-local structure to qubits, resulting in intricate connectivity requirements that are difficult for current quantum computers to replicate digitally. To circumvent this issue, an innovative hybrid approach has been proposed and experimentally implemented, combining pre-and post-mapping digital circuitry with analog simulations of the fermionic systems, analogous to the various representations of a lattice fermionic system. This analog component harnesses the inherent connectivity of the system, while its digital framework divides the problem into more manageable sections. Using a hybrid approach, an experiment was conducted on a 16-qubit superconducting quantum processor to investigate the dynamics of a 1D spin-1/2 fermionic system known as the Hubbard model, with the aim of obtaining an energy spectrum in agreement with exact diagonalization results.

Investigating how to build features for graph-based machine learning, particularly with large and complex real-world datasets, reveals a limitation in current feature construction methods, which often rely on pre-defined frameworks and struggle to capture the unique characteristics of each problem. To address this challenge, we developed real-world features from the ground up, analyzing several popular large-scale graph networks, and experimented with multiple feature types, such as node properties, random features, and the graph's topological structure, for a financial analysis task, and evaluated their effectiveness using the wealth feature as a case study in the financial network. The results showcase the potential for effective feature construction in graph-based machine learning, even with real-world data, and demonstrate that such features can improve the performance of the models. The study also provides a clear example of how to create meaningful features from the wealth, a real-world network, and demonstrates their utility in the financial analysis context. The findings are substantial, featuring an increase of 10% in the model's performance and providing a step towards addressing the dilemma of balancing optimization and generalization in graph-based machine learning. The study's approach is simple, yet effective, and can be applied to any graph, such as the airline network or the financial market, and leads to a significant improvement in the model's performance. The findings are substantial, featuring an increase of 10% in the model's performance and providing a step towards addressing the optimization-generalization dilemma in graph-based machine learning.

Achieving a precise focus on a single point within and beyond biological tissue is an intricate task, and producing a desired pattern inside low-scattering media like phantom tissue presents significant optical challenges. To tackle this issue, we have developed an efficient iterative system based on a nonλ/4-blank phase-type liquid crystal spatial light modulator, capable of simultaneously creating several complex patterns at different depths within low-scattering media like rabbit ear tissue, without requiring optimization of the phantom's scattering properties. This novel approach outperforms the standard iterative phase correction (IPC) method by light, and it has the capacity to correct mid-range scattering losses in low to mid-scattering materials, facilitating complex optical manipulations within biological samples.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by the editors and discussants, which allows for further exploration of our primary study, particularly its limitations. Our research aimed to develop a statistically efficient method for identifying personalized treatment strategies that minimize adverse effects. The proposed strategy is based on minimizing prediction errors for outcomes under different treatments, regardless of initial conditions. We are particularly interested in treatments that not only achieve optimal outcomes but also adapt to varying initial conditions. Although the initial proposed method is guaranteed to find such a treatment, its efficiency is a limitation. To address this issue, we propose a new method that maintains the same convergence rate as the original. This new method relies on having more data and initially proposes an estimator for the target parameter.

A proof-of-concept radiative cooling detector is being built as a testbed for monolithic small collection electrode technology, utilizing CLIC technology. The experimental setup is designed to be fully passively cooled, relying on radiative heat transfer. In building the detector testbed, research focused on optimizing the thickness of the thermoelectric material and the underlying substrate. Different materials for both layers were tested, with specific attention to their thermal and mechanical properties. Various designs, featuring both flexible and rigid substrates, were tested to determine the most effective method for achieving low temperatures with minimal power. The results indicate that using flexible polyimide substrates yield the lowest temperatures, particularly due to their thin profile. Moreover, utilizing indium tin oxide as the active layer material appears more efficient than gold.

As the collecting area of large telescopes grows, detector pixel sizes become limited by atmospheric turbulence, reducing the effective resolution even with advanced adaptive optics systems. The atmospheric self-coherent camera (ASCC) technique has shown promise in recovering high-resolution signals through the optimization of speckle patterns, but its real-world feasibility has not been fully confirmed. We have successfully implemented a new fast ASCC (fASCc) at the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (SCEAO) testbed and achieved remarkable results, including a signal recovery rate of up to 90% and connection probabilities close to 1.0, all within a 10 millisecond time frame. The integration of fASCc with a high-performance phase unwrapper enables its practical use in large telescope designs for connecting multiple photons.

The curve shifted Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model improves upon the traditional Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, which is limited to representing positive interest rates. Our study validates this model, developing mathematical proofs for bond pricing, pricing hedging strategies, and simulation methods. Model validation involves proving the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the partial differential equation governing the forward price, which also allows for the derivation of a unique solution to the partial differential equation used in pricing hedging strategies. Additionally, we establish the convergence in law of Monte Carlo simulations to the correct price and provide numerical examples to demonstrate the efficacy of our approaches.

In meta-analysis, particularly with multivariate data, cluster-robust standard errors are often utilized to mitigate issues such as network clustering, publication bias, and control for heteroscedasticity. The current study examines cluster-robust methods in bivariate meta-analysis under various scenarios, including fixed and random effects models. The investigation particularly focuses on the implications of ignoring random effects when estimating cluster-robust standards errors, and provides guidelines on when using such methods remains valid in bivariate meta-analysis. The analysis utilizes theoretical reasoning as well as simulations, which were applied to real-world examples.

In particle-resolved simulations with actual flight times and deformation times, the time it takes for particles to collide is significantly shorter than the time it takes for them to settle or deform, especially at high densities. This disparity poses a significant challenge to efficient multiple-time-step simulation, as accurately predicting particle collisions requires solving complex equations, while modeling particle interactions, such as settling and deformation, only requires solving simpler equations, allowing for longer time steps. We developed a new integration method that takes advantage of this disparity in the simulation of multiple particles, using fourth-order Runge-Kutta for collision and solving equations, and achieving time savings of over an order of magnitude at extremely high densities, with minimal loss of accuracy, as verified by comparing the results with a standard integration method.

In this paper, we provide an in-depth analysis of the particle energy balance for a black hole or uniformly accelerated system. We explore the concept that external work is necessary to sustain the continuous emission of radiation, which is a requirement in order for the black hole or accelerated system to emit radiation and lose energy. Additionally, we calculate the efficiency of this process.

We examine the influence of recoil effects on minijet cross sections in the context of the LHC, utilizing the color dipole model with a BFKL evolution kernel in saturation and a Gaussian distribution of color sources. Our analysis reveals a substantial recoil contribution, equivalent to the virtuality of the LHC, which accounts for a significant portion, approximately 30%, of the total minijet cross section.

This article offers a proof for identifying all integer triples of $a, b, n$ that satisfy the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, simultaneously providing a demonstration of its inherent properties as an exponential Diophantine equation.

Our study focused on analyzing fluctuations in a liquid jet that was introduced into a flowing jet within a channel. We investigated the effects of changing the liquid jet frequency and width on the flow disturbances within the channel. Our observations revealed heightened fluctuations in the flow as the liquid jet frequency and size increased. Notably, when the liquid jet frequency matched the flow speed divided by a characteristic length scale ($u/L$), we observed significant instability in the flow. This phenomenon resulted in the formation of vortices that rotated in the plane defined by the channel's width and the vertical axis. Furthermore, we noted instability developing in the flow both upstream and downstream of the point where the liquid jet was created. This effect was more pronounced when the width of the liquid jet was increased.

Recent developments in NVMMs bring with them the responsibility of ensuring that program results aren't corrupted, necessitating the upholding of crash consistency, i.e., program results must be consistent with some sequential execution point prior to the system crash. Although modern processors provide support for crash consistency, most existing memory models either neglect it entirely, as in the case of the ARMv8 model, or necessitate the adoption of unpractical solutions, like the strict total order required by the TBB model. In response, we've devised an innovative memory model centered on algorithm-directed crash consistency, which provides the system with the flexibility to specify its own crash consistency rules, offering both greater expressiveness and more precise control over results. Our framework, aligned with the principles of the ARMv8 memory model, introduces the notion of crash-consistent stores, as opposed to the existing concept of globally visible stores. We illustrate the efficacy of our model by demonstrating that, in many common scenarios, algorithm-directed crash consistency yields the same observable outcomes as strict total order, while also providing the freedom for programmers to specify their own crash consistency rules.

Over the years, network analysis has evolved from simple network models to complex multilayer systems. Hierarchies within networks have garnered significant attention in understanding complex systems, exemplified by organizational structures, governmental systems, and ecological frameworks. Despite the progress made, the computational methods for identifying hierarchical systems have yet to be thoroughly explored, especially in relation to the practical applications. This study presents two innovative and scalable algorithms for detecting hierarchical structures in large complex network datasets. The evaluation involves comparing the algorithms with existing methods on synthetic and real-world data, assessing their performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The study further evaluates the performance of these algorithms using specific metrics, including the conductance and purity of the identified modules at each level of the hierarchy.

We analyze the most widely accepted resolution to the three-body problem, the statistical prediction, in light of recent advancements in high-precision N-body simulations. By comparing the predicted flux of bound pairs and triples against those simulated, we find strong support for the statistical prediction across a range of parameters, such as the mass ratio and energy distribution. We also examine its applicability to systems with pre-established triples and consider its utility in understanding the dynamics of galactic globular clusters.

The PHENIX experiment at the RHIC collider analyzed the suppression of both bound, pre-existing, and newly formed charm-anticharm mesons in lead-lead collisions.  In central collisions, both types of charmonium showed significant suppression relative to proton-proton collisions, with central to peripheral trends matching those observed at higher energies.  Measurements also revealed that $\psi(2S)$ was suppressed more than $J/\psi$, exceeding expected thermal suppression in the first 100 picoseconds.  This suggests that suppression beyond the effects of cold hadronic collisions may be present.  However, since the experiment lacks a baseline for hadron-meson interactions, this possibility cannot be confirmed or ruled out definitively.

We develop a robust framework in continuous logic by defining a precise formulation of continuity and equality, and establishing a corresponding notion of Morley and Shahshani continuity. It is shown that any continuous first-order theory is equivalent to a specific topology on its models, and this topological structure is preserved under elementary reductions. Additionally, we outline strategies to integrate topological model theory into the framework of functorial and functorial topological model theory.

To optimize the efficiency of information processing in computing, singular value decomposition (SVD) is utilized. SVD has demonstrated effectiveness in enhancing the speed and accuracy of various information-related tasks. This paper investigates the application of SVD in parallelizing the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) method for test case selection in software systems. The proposed algorithm leverages SVD to partition the training data matrix into subspaces, which are then utilized to predict and evaluate test cases. The efficiency of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through numerical experiments on artificial and real-world datasets. The results indicate that the SVD-based parallel SSA algorithm effectively accelerates the SSA process and improves its accuracy and efficiency.

A new approach to monitoring for suicidal thoughts and behaviors in electronic health records is presented, leveraging advanced deep learning techniques. This method integrates sequential and tabular data from multiple sources, applying specific deep learning architectures to each: recurrent neural networks for sequential information and gradient boosting and neural networks for tabular information. The effectiveness of this approach in identifying suicidal thoughts and behaviors was evaluated using a large dataset of clinical encounters, starting from preliminary recurrent neural network models and building upon it by combining differentRecurrent Neural Networksrecurrent neural network models and the utilization of recurrent autoencoders for feature extraction. The performance of these models was evaluated using various evaluation metrics.
